subsubtopic: SUGGESTED REFORMS TO IMPROVE RELATIONSHIPS WITH EMPLOYEES-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43 on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity. It concerns the current dispute in the Toronto post office which, if not resolved immediately, could precipitate a work stoppage which would have a devastating effect on Canada's economy, which is already crippled by government mismanagement. 1 move, seconded by the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka (Mr. Darling):
That this House urges the government to proceed with urgently needed reforms in collective bargaining procedures in the public service which were proposed by the retiring chairman of the Public Service Staff Relations Board, Jacob Finkelman, over two years ago, and urges the Postmaster General to proceed with the long delayed reforms in the Post Office recommended by the Official Opposition which would introduce co-operation and co-determination by management, labour and postal users in post office administration, in place of the continuing confrontation which threatens to destroy Canada's once efficient postal service.

PROPOSED REINSTATEMENT OF SUSPENDED TORONTO EMPLOYEES-MOTION UNDER S O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I too rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43 concerning the vitally important matter of the postal dispute which is now taking place in the city of Toronto and which could tie up the total postal service across the country at this particularly serious time. In light of the fact that the particular dispute which caused this demonstration has been settled to the satisfaction of both sides and in light of the fact that the union is willing to cease picketing as soon as the suspended workers are reinstated, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles):
That the Postmaster General be instructed to reinstate immediately the nine suspended workers at the Toronto Central Post Office, and further that an independent adjudicator be appointed to investigate and make final recommendations regarding the suspension of the nine postal workers.

subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR AMENDMENT TO PROTECT PRIVACY OF CANDIDATES DURING ELECTION-MOTION UNDER S O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I too rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43 on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity. In light of the fact that section 16(3)(c) of the Official Secrets Act makes possible the authorization of wiretapping directly by the Solicitor General of Canada (Mr. Fox) without a judge's consent in connection with activities directed toward accomplishing governmental change within Canada or elsewhere by any criminal means- and I emphasize "any criminal means"-and in view of the complexities of the federal Canada Elections Act regarding the raising of money and other matters it is quite possible that a candidate for membership in the House of Commons could unintentionally break the law during election time and have his telephone tapped, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mr. Alexander):
That the government amend the said act by providing an exemption for any violation of the Canada Elections Act, as it has nothing to do with national security and therefore candidates in a federal election should be guaranteed privacy at their campaign headquarters and other places during federal elections.

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED INCREASE IN WRITEOFF OF COST OF RESEARCH-MOTION UNDER S O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to move a motion under Standing Order 43 on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity. As Canadian industry must greatly increase its industrial research if we are to lower our costs and improve our quality and design in order to begin to overcome the $11.5 billion per year adverse trade balance we now have in manufactured products, the ones which produce jobs, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Halton-Wentworth (Mr. Kempling):
That the government allow industry to write off 200 per cent of the cost of all current and capital expenditures on industrial research in excess of those made in the base year, the year before the plan goes into operation.
Such a program would induce the additional industrial research we need to make our manufactured products more competitive in the marketplace and capable of increasing sales production and jobs.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43 to present a motion on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity. In light of the tragic air crash at Churchill Falls on December 9, 1977 with the loss of eight lives which represents the second fatal crash for the company; in view of the conflict between Air Canada and MOT over the towing of jet aircraft and other equipment across two major runways at Winnipeg Airport to the new Air Canada hangar which will be a safety hazard, and the reported lack of air safety in northern Manitoba, involving illegally operating aircraft, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Provencher (Mr. Epp):
That this House direct the government House leader to provide a reference to the Standing Committee on Transport and Communications to launch a full scale investigation into aviation safety in Canada, and for the calling of any or all witnesses to appear before the committee.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43 on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity. In the statement, the minister said: "Let me first address myself to the question of whether or not I had any prior knowledge of the October 6-7, 1972, break-in at the APLQ. My answer to the question is a flat no." He further stated: "Had I prior knowledge of the operation, I would have intervened to prevent it from happening." Mr. Speaker, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Perth-Wilmot (Mr. Jarvis):
That this House requests the former Solicitor General, now the Minister of Supply and Services, to review his statement in this House on June 21 to determine if all matters referred to therein are still factually correct. subsubtopic: THREATENED STRIKE-GOVERNMENT ACTION TO AVOID
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Postmaster General. In light of his assurances that there would be no postal strike this Christmas and
Oral Questions
the recent statement by the president of the Canadian Union of Postal Workers that there would be no wildcat or national strikes during the Christmas season unless the employer provoked the union into a strike situation, can the hon. gentleman inform the House how the post office got itself into the present mess?

subsubtopic: THREATENED STRIKE-GOVERNMENT ACTION TO AVOID
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the hon. gentleman knows the series of events that led to the present impasse in Toronto. Indeed the reporting has been relatively accurate. If the hon. member had listened to the motion brought by the leader of the New Democratic Party under Standing Order 43 he would know exactly what led to this particular impasse. I want to advise the hon. gentleman that the discussions with the local leaders of CUPW are ongoing and I am still optimistic that we will have the matter resolved in the near future.

subsubtopic: THREATENED STRIKE-GOVERNMENT ACTION TO AVOID
speechtext: Inasmuch as the outstanding issue is the suspension of the nine employees, can the Postmaster General assure the House and the country that this grievance will be dealt with through the normal grievance procedures, rather than necessitating the usual resort to strike action.

subsubtopic: THREATENED STRIKE-GOVERNMENT ACTION TO AVOID
speechtext: As I have advised the hon. gentleman the matter will shortly be discussed with the union. We had discussions with the local union leadership over the weekend, both Saturday and Sunday. Indeed the issue which the hon. member has called to our attention is one under discussion. I would rather not comment until those discussions are fully underway and we are in a position to make a joint statement with the union.

subsubtopic: THREATENED STRIKE-GOVERNMENT ACTION TO AVOID
speechtext: In view of the vital importance of a reliable mail service to small business, to the recovery of an economy faced with high unemployment and inflation, and the general wellbeing of the country at a time of stress and strain in national unity, would the Postmaster General inform the House what special steps he is taking at this time to respond to the overwhelming demand from the long suffering Canadian public that the Christmas spirit not be destroyed by yet another postal strike? And would he use the goodwill of Christmas to assure his workers that he will introduce modern labour-management relations into the post office as has been advocated for a long time now by the official opposition.

subsubtopic: THREATENED STRIKE-GOVERNMENT ACTION TO AVOID
speechtext:
I am glad the hon. member has brought the Christmas spirit into his question. We are hopeful that that is perhaps going to be the determining factor in this instance. I call to the attention of the union and all hon. members of this House that we are, Mr. Speaker, in a very volatile situation, in a period of national life when emotions tend to be very high. Every effort that I and my officials can muster, will be used in order to pacify the situation and not inflame it so that indeed solutions can be arrived at reasonably by reasonable people.
I trust that the hon. gentleman by the very reasonable approach he is using this afternoon is going to use his own good offices in order to communicate with his friends within

December 12, 1977
Oral Questions
the post office to ensure that the spirit of goodwill will prevail and that we will be able to resolve this issue this afternoon, or as soon as possible, and get the mail moving again.

Thank you very much, Mr. Speaker. I am delighted to hear the Postmaster General talk of sweet reason.
However, if I may put this question to the Postmaster General: in the event of a complete breakdown in current negotiations, is the government preparing legislation to cope with the threat of a nationwide strike?

I can indicate to the hon. gentleman that the strike is illegal and is in contravention of the Public Service Staff Relations Act. I cannot see how the Parliament of Canada can impose another legality on a present illegal situation. I simply indicate to the hon. gentleman that the operations in Toronto are ongoing. There are interruptions now, but we have one post office operating and we have one postal installation operating without the intervention of pickets. There are pickets at two other main installations, but some of the trucks are crossing those pickets. We are attempting to carry on with the mail that is available to us in the hope that within a short period of time, after reasonable minds prevail we will have the system in full operation. For that I seek the co-operation of hon. gentlemen.

Mr. Speaker, it is also obvious that if we are to settle disputes we would need that the spirit of Christmas, which is essential at this time of the year, be not undermined and that people recognize that the important thing is to provide Canadians with a complete and efficient postal service during a period which carries so much feeling.

subtopic: ACTION TO ENSURE DELIVERY OF OLD AGE PENSION CHEQUES IN VIEW OF THREATENED STRIKE
ACTION TO ENSURE DELIVERY OF OLD AGE PENSION CHEQUES IN VIEW OF THREATENED STRIKE
speechtext: If I could pose a supplementary to the Postmaster General. What action has the government taken to ensure delivery of old age pension cheques and other government cheques on time, and what other emergency procedures has the government and the Postmaster General come up with to cope with this possible strike and ensure that Christmas mail will go through.

subtopic: ACTION TO ENSURE DELIVERY OF OLD AGE PENSION CHEQUES IN VIEW OF THREATENED STRIKE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member has identified that there are transfer payments that are presently in the post office. We have family allowances in the mail stream as well as provincial guaranteed annual income cheques. With that sort of valuable mail within the system and the dependence of recipients on the amounts that are forthcoming, especially during this Christmas season,

and the vulnerability of the small businessman which the hon. member has so well identified, I again publicly urge the national directors of the Canadian Union of Postal Workers to recognize the difficulties that we might be incurring if we leave this matter unresolved for a period of time.

subtopic: THREATENED STRIKE-REQUEST FOR REPORT ON INJUNCTION PROCEEDINGS
THREATENED STRIKE-REQUEST FOR REPORT ON INJUNCTION PROCEEDINGS
speechtext: On the question of the injunction requested by the Postmaster General, did the hon. gentleman approach the federal or the provincial judiciary and what is the current situation on this front?

subtopic: THREATENED STRIKE-REQUEST FOR REPORT ON INJUNCTION PROCEEDINGS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the application for the injunction was made to the Supreme Court of Ontario, as is normal under the circumstances. The hearing was adjourned in order that there might be negotiations under less pressure. We are going to resume the hearing tomorrow morning at nine o'clock and hope that in the meantime we might be able to make an arrangement.

subsubtopic: ALLEGED SURVEILLANCE OF NEW DEMOCRATIC PARTY- REQUEST FOR STATEMENT THAT ACTION UNWARRANTED
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Solicitor General. A report tabled in the Ontario Legislature on Friday by the attorney general of that province makes it clear that the RCMP carried on a systematic investigation not only of the Waffle group within the NDP but also of the party itself between 1970 and 1973. In his letter to me dated August 26 of this year the Solicitor General states that he agreed completely with a point I made in an earlier letter that the security branch should only be concerned with "groups believed to be committed to the use of non-democratic means in pursuit of their objectives". In light of this assertion, will he take this opportunity to assert publicly that this kind of systematic surveillance of democratic groups in Canada was totally unwarranted?

subsubtopic: ALLEGED SURVEILLANCE OF NEW DEMOCRATIC PARTY- REQUEST FOR STATEMENT THAT ACTION UNWARRANTED
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the position that I gave the leader of the New Democratic Party in the letter that I wrote to him is, of course, the position of the government. The RCMP has no mandate whatsoever to do any systematic surveillance of legitimate activities of any political party in Canada.

subsubtopic: ALLEGED SURVEILLANCE OF NEW DEMOCRATIC PARTY- REQUEST FOR STATEMENT THAT ACTION UNWARRANTED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the minister simply repeated what he said in his letter. I ask him to follow up his assertion, which I welcomed in the letter, with a judgment about the revelation that has been produced in the legislature in the province of Ontario, namely that the RCMP security branch between 1970 and 1973 kept systematic surveillance of the activities of the Waffle group within the NDP and, indeed, the New Democratic Party itself during that time. If that is the case, I
December 12, 1977

would like the Solicitor General of Canada to make his civil liberties position well-known at this time and to say that that kind of activity is something of which he disapproves.

subsubtopic: ALLEGED SURVEILLANCE OF NEW DEMOCRATIC PARTY- REQUEST FOR STATEMENT THAT ACTION UNWARRANTED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have not seen the report that the hon. member refers to which has been tabled in the Ontario legislature. To my knowledge at the moment, there is no information to indicate that the New Democratic Party was the object of systematic surveillance, as the leader of that party puts it in the House today, during that period of time.
There may or may not have been some surveillance of individual members, as we have stated time and again in the House. The fact that one belongs to a political party does not give one immunity from surveillance if there is reason to believe there may be cause for surveillance along the lines I indicated to the hon. member in the letter he is now quoting back to me.

subsubtopic: ALLEGED SURVEILLANCE OF NEW DEMOCRATIC PARTY- REQUEST FOR STATEMENT THAT ACTION UNWARRANTED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I find it strange the minister is not aware of the specifics that went into that report. The letter is some months old from the attorney general of that province to the Solicitor General making inquiries about this subject matter. This was followed up, I understand, by the attorney general of the province of Ontario when he was not satisfied with the reply the Solicitor General gave him some time ago. It was followed up with officials within the RCMP. The report is as a result of information provided to the attorney general of that province by the RCMP within the minister's own department. In that report, the attorney general of the province of Ontario said that the inquiries "were broadened sufficiently to put the activities of these individuals in proper perspective". That is a reference to the investigation of the Waffle group being broadened within the framework of the NDP itself.
That is a sheer euphemism for saying that the party itself was being investigated. I therefore ask the minister to assure us that the New Democratic Party were not under surveillance between 1970 and 1973 in a systematic way. Will he clear up the point that is of concern to hundreds of democratically oriented Canadians who were taking part in that Waffle group that they were not in any way indulging in any subversive activities? Will he assert once again that he sees a distinction between dissent and subversion-

subsubtopic: ALLEGED SURVEILLANCE OF NEW DEMOCRATIC PARTY- REQUEST FOR STATEMENT THAT ACTION UNWARRANTED
speechtext: Oh, go on!

subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR STATEMENT BY MINISTER OUTLINING PROBLEMS IN FINANCING, LABOUR RELATIONS AND ADMINISTRATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to address my question to the Postmaster General
Oral Questions
and refer him to a news release from the Canadian Union of Postal Workers-I know he has seen it-in which the opinion is expressed that the Postmaster General has not been bargaining in good faith and that he has been hiding the facts. The news release goes on to say that because of the attitude of the Postmaster General the union will continue to do everything in its power to inform the public, the information media and all its members as to the solutions which must be adopted in order to resolve problems within the Post Office involving administration, labour relations and financing. Since the union is prepared to do this, is the minister willing to make a statement on motions as soon as possible, preferably before Christmas, making clear just what the problems are in relation to administration, labour relations and finance so that Canadians may know just what is going on? After all, they are paying a very high price for service they are not getting.

subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR STATEMENT BY MINISTER OUTLINING PROBLEMS IN FINANCING, LABOUR RELATIONS AND ADMINISTRATION
speechtext: I thank the hon. member for providing me with an opportunity of making a clarification. The press release from which he has read is one which was issued by the President of CUPW after I had made an application for the appointment of a conciliation board in connection with the main negotiations between the parties which are being conducted at the national level. The hon. member will recall that in the press conference which followed that press release Mr. Parrot did say that in his view there would be no interruption of the mails before Christmas. He was referring to the main negotiations between the Post Office and CUPW in connection with the renewal of the collective agreement which terminated on June 30. The questions to which I was replying earlier concerned a different situation, one which has arisen at the Toronto local, and I would beg the hon. gentleman not to mix up the two situations. The dispute at Toronto is completely separate and apart from the main negotiations.

subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR STATEMENT BY MINISTER OUTLINING PROBLEMS IN FINANCING, LABOUR RELATIONS AND ADMINISTRATION
speechtext: I am not mixed up. The Postmaster General is mixed up. I am simply pointing out that people are paying exorbitant prices for services they are not getting. We understand, now, that there are problems. I will read the press release again because it seems the Postmaster General was not listening. Mr. Parrot said there were problems in the Post Office in connection with labour relations, administrative matters and financial matters and that the union intended to bring those problems to the attention of the Canadian public so that they would know what is going on. All 1 am asking the Postmaster General is to stand up on motions, without giving us any lessons, and make a complete and definite statement as to what is going on in the Post Office so that the Canadian people may know where they are going. The service is costing a lot of money and there is no assurance of mail delivery.

subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR STATEMENT BY MINISTER OUTLINING PROBLEMS IN FINANCING, LABOUR RELATIONS AND ADMINISTRATION
speechtext:
Two or three weeks ago at most I made a statement on motions and subjected myself to inquiries from opposition members. If the hon. member, in his belated interest in the Post Office, had been concerned then he could have directed questions to me at that time. I was here, and I replied to questions by opposition members and some of those ques-

December 12, 1977
Oral Questions
tions were directed to the problems we face in the Post Office. For the hon. member for Hamilton West to try to reveal all of a sudden that there are problems in the Post Office seems to be rather strange. I wonder where he has been since 1975. In 1975 we had a 42-day strike. We have had some interruptions from time to time, but I have indicated to hon. members opposite exactly the measures we were taking. One of those measures is to avoid inflaming a situation by making unsubstantiated statements and by engaging in dialogue with CUPW in surroundings which are more conducive to agreements and arrangements than in confrontation, as the hon. member is suggesting.

subsubtopic: POSSIBILITY OF USING POWDERED MILK IN PROCESSING OF FEED GRAIN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Agriculture.
Considering that a number of industrial milk producers will be without any income for several months because they have met their production quotas, and considering also that the Canadian Dairy Commission is selling powdered milk on the world market below the Canadian support price, which will inevitably involve considerable expenses both for milk producers and for the state, would the minister tell the House whether he has ordered research into a greater use of milk powder in the processing of feed grain as a way of reducing powdered milk stocks?

speakeroldname: Hon. E. F. Whelan (Minister of Agriculture):
subsubtopic: POSSIBILITY OF USING POWDERED MILK IN PROCESSING OF FEED GRAIN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker,
I am sure the hon. member knows that skim milk powder is being used in many, many different products today. It is highly nourishing. We are doing more research. If the hon. member has any suggestions as to how it can be used, we would be pleased to hear them also. This year in Canada skim milk powder is being subsidized by practically a third or more of its cost, yet consumption went down. I do not know the reason. It was provided in Canada cheaper than in any other country of the world.
[ Translation]

subsubtopic: POSSIBILITY OF USING POWDERED MILK IN PROCESSING OF FEED GRAIN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a supplementary question. I think either I did not make myself perfectly clear or the minister did not want to understand the
(Mr. Blais.)
meaning of my question. It was obviously a suggestion I was making in putting this question, because these suggestions come from feed grain producers themselves. Has some research been done on that by Department of Agriculture researchers who are given a budget for that? Did they study the possiblity of using more powdered milk in processing feed grain as well as the effects it will have on the prices of feed? It is only after this kind of study that we will be able to see whether it will be advantageous or not.

subsubtopic: POSSIBILITY OF USING POWDERED MILK IN PROCESSING OF FEED GRAIN
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, research is continuing in our department and research is continuing in the private sector. The government has allocated $4 million for research into all dairy products and not just skim milk powder. Part of that money is being used for research into different ways to use skim milk powder in the baking industry and for total human consumption. There are many ways it can be improved. There is a tremendous amount of skim milk powder, and I do not think Canadians could consume it all. Prime Minister said, "Yes, Mr. Speaker." Since returning here this morning I see from the Ottawa Journal, in which the earlier report appeared, that someone called Richard O'Hagan in the Prime Minister's office says it was all a misunderstanding. He said it was one of those half distracted answers and that one could not have listened without wondering if he knew what he was replying to. This is quite an explanation-that the Prime Minister in the question period is distracted and does not know what he is listening to and does not know what he is replying to.
This is an apparently incorrect answer on a serious matter, given by the Prime Minister. It affects the United States and must be embarrassing to the U.S. ambassador. I personally do not agree with the statement of the Minister of Agriculture that the ambassador is running around and should not be talking about free trade. I think he is entitled to talk about what he likes and that he is quite an outstanding representative of the United States. The Prime Minister has not told the House that this was a mistake of his, a wrong statement, and that no diplomatic note has been sent. I raise this question now because I think it is a breach of our privileges and is certainly not calculated to improve relations between this country and the United States of America of which the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Jamieson) is so fond. Could we have the record straightened out?
