speakeroldname: Hon. Allan J. MacEachen (for the Minister of Finance) moved
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext: that Bill C-ll, to amend the statute law relating to income tax and to provide other authority for the raising of funds, be read the third time and do pass.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on November 7 I replied to the minister on second reading of this
Income Tax
bill. Since that time we have heard the minister repeat ad nauseam, and quite frankly in a way that I think is totally unworthy of him, that he had been sitting here listening to debate on this bill for 32 or 33 days and that he has been forced to move closure on two occasions because the debate has taken an unconscionable length of time.
Just for the uninitiated I have before me a copy of Bill C-ll. It contains some 100 clauses, with 225 pages of text. It covers a great diversity of sections within the Income Tax Act. For example it introduces amendments to the Old Age Security Act. Then, lo and behold, just a little trailer, well hidden under the back end of what you might call this huge vehicle, is an increase in borrowing authority of $9 billion. Well, the former minister of finance had tried to tuck it in on another occasion in an appropriation bill for supplementary estimates, where there was no opportunity to debate the increase in this borrowing limit. Fortunately, we spotted that attempted bootlegging. And it was a straight bootleg, Mr. Speaker, of an authority which would be slipped through the House. I am sure there was not even two members on the backbench who were aware of it-possibly the Cabinet knew about it; certainly the Minister of Finance knew about it; and possibly the parliamentary secretary. That is dishonest government. Legislation should not be handled this way when it deals with more than one particular statute and becomes an omnibus bill.
Certainly there are different principles involved in this bill. I would like to know, Mr. Speaker, just what might be the principle of it. It is described as an act to amend Income Tax. It comes into the Committee of the Whole as provided for by the rules of the House. All other legislation should go to committee, but a provision to amend the borrowing authority of the government is tacked on to this bill illegally, I suggest, because of the principle of it not being an amendment to the Income Tax Act but an increase in the borrowing authority.
There are changes in the Old Age Security Act included. Therefore the bill then becomes an act to amend a number of statutory enactments. Under that guise it should not be in this House but in the Committee of the Whole. The House cannot have it both ways.
I did not speak on a point of order at second reading with regard to this matter, nor did I speak in the debate on closure, but I am going to have a good deal to say about closure with regard to this bill. In the House over the past month a picture of misrepresentation was given. What else could the minister expect than what has happened during the past month?
We commenced in October with the Throne Speech debate. It was interrupted on October 21 on the Thursday of the first week of debate by a mini-budget, which in itself should have had a six-day debate. But no, it was bootlegged into the middle of another debate, which by tradition gives ministers and members of this House an opportunity to canvass conditions socially and economically, generally or in particular-whatever their choice may be.

December 12, 1977
Income Tax
On top of that along came the INCO lay-offs one day later, October 21, and Mr. Speaker refused a motion under Standing Order 26 saying that the matter could be discussed during the Throne Speech debate. Of course it could. Of course it was, but I think improperly. There was ample opportunity to use Standing Order 26 for sittings at night to discuss the whole question, instead of directing that a debate should take place with regard to a particular subject to the prejudice of other members. There were many members, Mr. Speaker, who were deprived of their right to speak during the Throne Speech debate because of those two actions, the introduction of the mini-budget and, secondly, the deliberate intrusion into the debate of the INCO situation which should have been handled in a different way.
Therefore when Bill C-ll came up for debate, many members who wanted to touch on subjects which were germane to income tax spoke on second reading, and the debate was there. The material was there. When was this going to be debated later? Next spring? The situation was now, and one could readily expect that the debate on second reading would be extensive. As reported at page 661 of Hansard, during second reading I said:
I hope some of the provisions will merit the fate they deserve and be defeated in the Committee of the Whole.
There were some very minor changes, but they do not go nearly far enough because the minister has had the temerity- I would not say gall-to use closure in committee of the whole. He is faced with this intriguing process. For purposes of information, he tabled a number of amendments to sections which were not reached before the guillotine fell. The net result is that he could not present his amendments or have them moved by one of his colleagues so that even without debate the House could consider the amendments.
In the end this bill will pass. The amendments will have to be introduced in the other place, and the bill-if they pass it there-will have to come back here for approval as amended by the other place. Of course those amendments will then be subject to debate. What does the minister hope to gain? He gains nothing by the premature use of the guillotine.
Let us look at how much time was taken up by the debate on second reading. There was a total of 27 hours and 20 minutes from November 7 to November 24, with interruptions for opposition days and Remembrance Day. On Monday, November 7, there was two hours and 53 minutes of debate; Tuesday, November 8, three hours and 14 minutes; Wednesday, November 9, two hours and 32 minutes-

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext: Too much time.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Members opposite feel there is too much time spent on legislation. They have not even seen it. They are not interested in it. Their participation in legislation is nil.
On Thursday, November 10, there was one hour and 18 minutes of debate; Monday, November 14, three hours and 25

minutes; Tuesday, November 15, opposition day; Wednesday, November 16, two hours and 23 minutes; Thursday, November 17, three hours and ten minutes; Friday, November 18, two hours and 30 minutes; Monday, November 21, two hours and 45 minutes, for a total debate on second reading of 24 hours and ten minutes.
There was a time allocation debate of two hours and 17 minutes. On Tuesday, November 22, there was the grand total of 30 minutes. On Wednesday ther was no debate because it was an opposition day. On Thursday, November 24, there were three hours and ten minutes. Therefore there was a total of 27 hours and 20 minutes for the bill, and two hours and 18 minutes for time allocation.
Let us look at committee of the whole. On Thursday, November 24, after the vote there were eight minutes; Friday, November 25, two hours and 56 minutes; Monday, November 28, three hours and 52 minutes; Tuesday, no debate, opposition day; Wednesday, November 30, two hours and 54 minutes; Thursday, December 1, three hours 40 minutes; Friday, December 2, opposition day; Monday, December 5, the debate on the allocation of time, two hours and five minutes, and then 30 minutes in committee; Thursday, December 6, three hours and 28 minutes; Wednesday, December 7, one hour and 42 minutes; Thursday, December 8, last opposition day; Friday, December 9, two hours and 50 minutes, for a committee stage total of 22 hours and one minute on a 225 page bill with more than 100 clauses.
Do members opposite have any idea of what is income tax and the number of subjects covered? How can they say we have spent too much time on this bill considering that it covered the income tax provisions of the March 31 budget plus the so-called budget in October? I am sorry, it was not March 31 but June, because it was in July that we passed certain amendments to the March 31 budget, if my memory serves me right.
During that time we did raise certain subjects that merit a great deal of attention. I am sorry that the government members did not feel persuaded to read in particular clause 75 of Bill C-22 passed in July under the guillotine, whereby it is a condition for purchasing and cashing Canada's Savings Bonds that the owner thereof shall have a social insurance number. This is nothing but pure bureaucracy run rampant.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
It is totally contrary to the words of the late Prime Minister Pearson when introducing the concept of social insurance numbers some 13 years ago. Not only that, but the forms for purchase of this year's Canada Savings Bonds provide for the inclusion of a social security number. All the minister said is that we have been using them here and using them there, and they are on the income tax forms. There have been a number of salami slices from time to time, and some of their use is absolutely debatable. The use of the social insurance number is not compulsory at this time. There are thousands upon thousands of senior citizens, married women who have never had employment and children who
December 12, 1977

are too young to take employment who are the owners of Canada Savings Bonds. In future they cannot cash any coupons on Canada Savings Bonds without obtaining a social insurance number.
I have had scores of elderly persons come to me. Frankly, a number of them never had to have a social insurance number. They retired before the social insurance number scheme was even introduced. Therefore there was absolutely no need for them to have a number.
I invite hon. members on both sides of the House to examine the application form and the requirements and the instructions for obtaining a social insurance number. With the rush that is now on, in many instances there is a delay of three to four weeks. It is centralized in some office over on Riverside Drive.
The law does not state that one has to have a social insurance number. Why should a housewife who has never worked and has no intention of working be forced to take a social insurance number if a husband or a relative makes her a gift of Canada Savings Bonds, or if she should inherit them?
What about children? It is one of the better habits of parents that can afford it, and it is surprising how many can, to start their teenage children on the useful pattern of saving by giving them a Canada Savings Bond or two. It used to be one could get them for $50. Now they cost $100. It sounds somewhat ludicrous that a 12-year-old child should get a $100 bond as a birthday gift, but with inflation that kind of value is no longer strange. Yet what else could one do in order that a child might get interest?
I thought, speaking privately to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien), that he had not heard of this particular provision when it went through as part of the March budget. I spoke out on second reading, but it is evident he soon hardened his mind. I must say it is my intention, if my bill is reached-I have a private member's bill already on the order paper-to seek the repeal of that section. I hope there will be an opportunity to have the subject debated because I am sure that the correspondence and telephone calls I have received duplicate those which have come to the attention of almost every member in this House.
I am against the principle that there should be this watchdog over me and over everyone else in the country in the form of a social insurance number. It is wrong. Oh, it is nice from the point of view of the bureaucrat, but it has been proven time and time again that anything which is administratively convenient deserves to be looked at three times, not twice, and I am sure this system is likely to infringe upon the ordinary rights of the citizens.
We are getting so wrapped up in controls of one form or another, whether at the federal level or at the provincial and municipal levels, that we can scarcely call our souls our own. 1 think people are fed up with this, totally and utterly fed up with it. And it is time we did something about it.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Hear, hear!
Income Tax

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext: The government is for the benefit of the people, it is not the people for the benefit of the government and those who administer government.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
If that is what qualifies me as a Conservative then I am proud to be a Conservative when I say those words.
My hon. friend from York-Simcoe led a long fight with regard to the taxation of income benefits from insurance policies. There was, it is true, a retreat from the proposals contained in the original June budget; I am glad to say the minister did withdraw, the result, I imagine, of pressure from his own back benches as well as from pressure by members on this side.
Insurance looms very large in the minds of the citizens of this country who are not rich, and often not in receipt of moderately high incomes. There are many, many people who pay in a pittance on small policies which represent their conception of how they can best put money aside within their means, modest as they may be. These savings provide a well of investment funds for this country to use-they would amount to a great deal more if the state at all three levels did not take 43 per cent of the gross national product, in which case a lot more money would be available for insurance and investment by the people generally, and they would not then be obliged to rely on the great, God-Almighty state to provide for them after retirement.
Somebody asked me today: Do you think the demand for social services, homes for the aged, day care centres and so on, is the result of government action? Mr. Speaker, it is hard to say which is the chicken and which is the egg. Is it because we are now in the seventies that we feel the state should have the responsibility of looking after each and every one of us beyond the age of 65, and that it should also have the responsibility of providing facilities for the care of children while they are of pre-school and elementary school age? Is that the state of our society today?
To get back to the subject of insurance and taxing the benefits thereof, certainly there have been changes. Even now, the minister has backed away from the idea that interest for a loan from an insurance company would not be counted as an expense of business if the money had been borrowed for the purpose of carrying on the business. I think the original proposal was nitpicking, a process of making it more difficult for citizens who must comply with the Income Tax Act. There are too many examples of this.
Take the loans for the purpose of home insulation. What a joke! They are subject to agreement by all the provinces and are subject to a maximum limit of $350 restricted to homes built prior to 1941. I understand that some of the provinces may make supplementary loans or grants. But it is all subject to income tax. What incentive is there, Mr. Speaker? What encouragement is there to insulate a home at a cost probably in excess of $350 in many cases only to find that the money, when eventually received, is subject to tax?

Income Tax
We want as many people to insulate their homes in order to conserve energy. The principle of the plan is quite good, if we want to save energy. I have saved energy. I doubled the insulation in my home this year, and I spent the $350 on an aluminum door. My wife has told me that already it is very apparent that we are going to save a fair amount on our heating bill this winter. Even with the severe cold and heavy snows we have had so far, the house is much more comfortable. Why tax the plan? I regret that part of this particular bill.
I had hoped to see much more in the way of incentives in this bill. There are some incentives, hopefully for scientific research. The hon. member for Wellington (Mr. Maine) spoke in this debate earlier. Of course he stressed, as a caveat, that there should not be bureaucratic bungling or the insistence on so many rules that, no matter how well-intentioned the plan, it would be totally negatived by the philosophy that a good idea must be smothered with paper work. I might not agree with the hon. member on a lot of things, but on this one idea I do.
There are a number of other subjects which will be covered by my colleagues in this third reading debate. I do not promise it will be short, because closure is counter-productive.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext: Right on.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext: If there has been a few more days allowed for consideration by committee of the whole, third reading would have been a matter of formality.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext: Oh, oh!

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext: The hon. "kid freshmen" in the back benches on the government side speak as if they are wise veterans in this House. They have not seen the operation of this House from both sides. I learned about parliamentary procedure when I was a parliamentary secretary on the other side and from sitting in the chair. This House has a certain temper. By agreement between House leaders legislation moves. There is far more achieved by consensus between House leaders. I have participated in a lot of negotiations conducted in that manner.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext: Since 1867.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext: After the hon. member is here another two months, he will change his mind, because two months is a relatively long time to him. If there is agreement between the House leaders, legislation will move. The worst one can do is impose the guillotine. It has been used fairly frequently of late. I suggest to hon. members that its continued use will be counter-productive. Government members have been invited to speak, to participate and to represent the ideas of their constituents. Far too many of them indicate the representation of their constituents in important legislation by sitting in their seats and remaining silent.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext: They do not express themselves in caucus; they do not look at the legislation in caucus.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext: When did the hon. member even sit in government caucus?

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext: We can hear you through the wall.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Government caucus is less important than opposition caucus. Hon. members opposite should find time to participate in caucus. They should ask their fellow members to participate, and then they will see how much time is spent.
I do not like this bill because of the number of things it does and because of some of the things it has omitted to do. I do not intend to vote for it.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I agree with one thing that the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) said, and that is on the problems which have developed as a result of the use of closure in regard to this tax bill.
The government had a large number of amendments which it wanted to incorporate in the bill, but it was unable to incorporate most of them. In fact seven or eight essential amendments should have been incorporated, but most of the government amendments did not get into the bill. There were approximately 70 or 80 amendments to this bill, most of them from the government side.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext: No.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext: Am I wrong?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext: You are wrong.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext: Well, there were 40, 70 or 80. It seems to me there were a lot, because on two or three occasions thick sheafs of amendments were tabled. At least there were 25 or 30.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext: Less than 30.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
In any case, this bill was so bad that the government wanted to amend it in a number of ways. Perhaps this is the help the government receives from its backbenchers. If that is so, they deserve all the more credit. Backbenchers on the government side should be aware of the fact that their input has been restricted because of closure, and many of the proposed amendments did not get into this legislation.
A tax bill is an important piece of legislation. It is certainly important to the government and to the country, and if there ever were a time when the country needed help, it is now. I think that the major problem in Canada, now with 1.5 million unemployed, is the creation of jobs, and one of the things which the income tax system can achieve is to change the distribution of income, usually by providing those who are in a position to make more income with the possibility of making
December 12, 1977

more purchases, thus creating more jobs. That is not what the government has done.
The government said that what we have to do is to give corporations a sum of money which will allow them, as one hon. member said, to modernize their production facilities, and to provide incentives to them to increase their production so that more people can be employed. What the government has allocated for that purpose under this tax bill is $1.2 billion. Opposition members and Liberal backbenchers should have said to the government that that is not the way to do it. The 1.2 billion will not increase productivity but will go into savings. It cannot go either into increasing productivity or into modernization. It is estimated that, on the average, production capacity in Canada is operating at about 80 per cent.
One of the clauses in the bill which we did not reach because of closure makes this clear, and I am sure that some government members have done surveys and would be able to indicate to the government that it was making a mistake in spending $1.2 billion to increase our production capacity when already we are operating at only 80 per cent of that capacity. This has resulted in very few jobs in the past. Other incentives of a similar nature have not produced much in the way of jobs.
There are many people who are in great need of consumer goods and in great need of housing. In fact they are in need of almost all goods that our factories can produce, yet they do not have the money with which to purchase these goods. If these budget resolutions now translated into this tax bill were to produce jobs in Canada they would have to do so by reducing the income tax of those who do not have enough money with which to buy the goods which they need, and which are necessary to provide jobs and to increase our productive capacity. We have not done that. Again we are providing corporations with assistance which we know will not be of much help in that respect. The only justification for this is that they have contributed heavily to a particular political party during an election, and $1.2 billion might probably be well spent in that regard.
We did discuss several clauses of the bill and it seems to me that one of them had a great deal to do with the unity of our nation, namely, the provisions regarding the insulation program. This program could not be better designed to divide the country if Rene Levesque had decided to bring in that kind of legislation himself. People in one part of Canada do not get the same breaks as people in another part of Canada.
We have a joint program in Prince Edward Island and Nova Scotia under which the people in those two provinces will receive $500 to insulate their houses, but in other parts of Canada, such as in Ontario, people cannot receive money to insulate a house unless it was built before 1921, and the maximum amount is only $350. This is a small program. Anyone who has bought any insulation material or done any insulation work on his property will know that $350 does not go very far. Now it is to be considered as part of one's taxable income anyway, so it will not amount to a full $350 for the purpose unless you have no income. And if you have no income, you could make better use of the $350 than to use it to
Income Tax
insulate your house because you would probably be using wood to heat the house, and the more wood you cut, the less wood you will need because you get warm cutting wood.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext: Is the hon. member suggesting we should burn our houses?

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
This is probably what the hon. member from New Brunswick believes. He is probably the kind of man who would do that. He is probably too lazy to shift his ass to cut down wood for burning so he would probably burn his house. I hope he does not decide to burn his neighbour's house as well. He has not had experience in cutting wood, although he comes from a province where there is wood and where people do cut down wood. The point I am making is not for that kind of member. He will go his own happy way to Brockville one of these days anyway, so we will not have to worry about him.
We are interested in having uniform programs across the country so that a Canadian in New Brunswick will not have to burn down his house to keep warm. People in New Brunswick, in British Columbia or in Prince Edward Island should have the same kind of insulation program.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I rise on a point of order? To begin with, the hon. member who has just been wasting the time of the House has used some very unparliamentary language.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext: I am prepared at any time to put up my knowledge and ability in wood cutting against the hon. member's abilities in that regard, and I am also willing to put up my knowledge of the bill. The hon. member has just referred to some 80 amendments. There were only 26 amendments proposed, 15 of which have been passed, and 11 of which are very technical amendments. If he wants to participate in this debate, he should stick to facts instead of making erratic statements.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
I did not identify the hon. member. He identified himself in his remarks. If the shoe fits him, let him wear it. If the hon. member has something to say, he should stand up and make a speech like anyone else. It seems to me that we have given him credit which he does not deserve.
The point I was trying to make is that if we are interested in establishing unity in this country, sooner or later we will have to establish an insulation program that will be made available to all Canadians at the same price, that will operate in the same way and that will provide the same benefits to all. Frankly, I think we should establish such a program because it is an excellent way of reducing the heating bill, but if we are to have a program, not only should we be able to assist people in insulating their homes but we should ensure that there are not rip-offs by producers of insulation material.
There are insulation shortages in many areas. In the last two years the increase in the cost of insulation has been fantastic.

December 12, 1977
Income Tax
It behooves the national government to set more rigid production standards than we now have. We have quite often found, after re-examination of insulation, that specifications have been considerably lower than they should have been. There are facilities for testing the R factor, but they are not good enough, and we are being ripped off. We have found that the standards set for insulation have not been met.
Everyone is interested in heating, and we should be giving some consideration to the specifications of electricity, oil, gas, and all the other fuels which are used. While the R factor for insulation has been checked and been found wanting, it is also true that at peak periods Ontario Hydro does not provide the same heating capacity as it does at other periods. Electricity with a factor close to 120 volts, bought several years ago can be reduced in stages of two volts at a time, bringing it down probably four or six volts. Anyone who has electric heating can find at certain times, no matter what their thermostats indicate, that their heating units are not operating at nearly the capacity they do at other times.
This is also true with gas. The BTU rating of gas was considerably higher when gas was first brought to Ontario by Trans-Canada than it is today. Since that time plants using that raw material have been established. They have been able to take out high energy materials such as butane so that a person buying fuel today quite often finds that it does not produce the same number of BTU's as it did previously. We should be able to control those factors. If we are going to subsidize the re-insulation of houses we should guarantee that people get what they pay for.
We should also be providing some benefit to those who buy small cars with small motors. This would bring about a saving in fuel, which will without a doubt be necessary before too long.
Other problems with regard to the Income Tax Act have been discussed at some length. One matter was the roll-over of property. There should certainly be no objection to taxing the capital gain which may result from a roll-over of property, but in addition to expropriations there are other occasions when we should give people at least two years to buy a second property. We have allowed one year for those who have to move for one reason or another.
Ordinary people who get involved in roll-overs are not speculating and are not wanting to make any particular gain, but through the death of a spouse or through inability, because of age or poor health, to operate a business, whether it be a farm or a small business, a person may have to acquire other property he can manage. Two years is an arbitrary figure, and even it would not necessarily allow for changes which are made necessary. A two-year period quite often might work a hardship.
There are a number of changes proposed in this tax bill. Normally a tax bill has very little appeal, but this one seems to have some for larger companies. We are making it possible for large companies to do things which are not necessarily in our interest. At second reading the hon. member for Waterloo-Cambridge (Mr. Saltsman) pointed out that many problems

have developed as a result of giving corporations and small businesses more money than they can spend. When that happens businesses increase savings and, as the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) said the other day, we may be saving ourselves right out of business. I read in a newspaper the other day that Canadians have S285 billion tied up in insurance plans.
When we give money to corporations and that money is retained by them, we find the same thing that is happening in the resource sector. Last week it was announced that 750 miners are to be laid off at Falconbridge. Prior to that 4,000 lay-off notices were given to employees of INCO at Sudbury, Thompson, Port Colborne and Timmins. Aid should be given to the resource sector to help it develop new mining propositions and new sawmills, and to help it modernize. However, when a mine or forest industry develops, management has some control over profits. Mining companies have the control of people's resources. They have some control over the costs involved in the development of resources because they can either "high grade" or "low grade". It is not impossible to know approximately how many tons of ore are available in a particular place and what the price for that ore might be. If the price of the product goes up, the amount of ore can be increased because low-grade ore can be mined. On the other hand, if the price of the ore drops, high grade ore can be mined; in other words, they use only the ore which produces a profit on the international market.
This bill would give companies like INCO a 3 per cent increase on their inventories. I agree that for manufacturing industries this is for the most part necessary. This means that if companies replace their inventories, this 3 per cent will help compensate for the inflationary trend which has developed over the period they have been holding their inventories. However, INCO, Falconbridge, Texas Gulf and other companies have built up inventories of base materials, paid overtime, and produced too much. They now have large inventories. It has been said that Sudbury has a seven or eight month inventory at the present time.
We paid a 3 per cent allowance to INCO to provide for that inventory inflation which they were already able to control by the type of ore they were mining. With the huge profit they had accumulated, the undistributed dividends and taxes they had been able to defer, they decided-and from a corporate point of view there is nothing wrong-to take their mining venture to Guatemala and Indonesia. With the help of export credits and of some other federal agencies they established themselves in countries that will allow them to compete with their own development in Canada. The result is that workers have been laid off in Canada, in many cases permanently, and the indication is that unless the world market increases within a relatively short time they will close the Canadian operations completely.
Miners are very important people, Mr. Speaker. We sometimes forget that there are only 750,000 miners, forest work-
December 12, 1977

ers, farmers and fishermen who provide all the wealth of this nation. Except in the financial area of lending money and collecting interest, all our wealth comes from these basis resources. The other ten million or so workers in one way or another are parasites on these industries. Now we find that 4,000 or 5,000 miners may be laid off permanently, and as well we have almost lost that many by attrition. We may soon find that communities supporting these industries are not viable, and that not only 4,000 or 5,000 people will be affected but rather up to 80,000 or 90,000 people who rely on the resultant business.
In spite of the mistakes of the past this income tax bill offers little help. The personal expense allowance has been doubled, but inflation has increased the cost of tools and expenses of the job by about 50 per cent, so this year workers would need $150 just to break even. The worker does not really receive any benefit from this provision and so cannot increase consumption to any degree. It was argued during debate that where it was absolutely necessary for a worker to drive long distances to and from the job, an allowance should be made for this, but the government refused. Concessions have been made to corporations and professional people but not to the working person.
If we are to receive any benefit from a budget and the income tax bills that flow from it, our purchasing power must be increased and jobs provided for those seeking them. These things should be the main purposes of a budget and I hope the Minister of Finance will bring one in without delay. Unless the young people of the country are assured of jobs we will have failed them and ourselves. No country of only ten million workers is rich enough to carry one and a half million unemployed for very long. The burden on the workers is too great and they will revolt. The one and a half million people looking for jobs that are not available will revolt as well, and we will all suffer the consequences. If we could decide on a redistribution of purchasing power perhaps we could eliminate this. Now is the time to look at redistributing the income of the ordinary Canadian rather than looking at handouts to the corporate welfare bums.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in speaking on third reading of Bill C- 111 recognize that in one way we are simply debating with a ghost, namely, the former minister of finance who provided the bulk of these proposals. We have to direct some remarks to the present minister, however, because there was a mini-budget since then.
I should like to start with the question of closure on a tax bill. I do not happen to believe in the principle of closure in a free parliament, and one of the reasons for that was demonstrated in this debate. Rightly or wrongly, this party decided to support the bill on second reading. If my memory is correct I sat in this House for a good many days on second reading and saw the debate winding to a close. We had only a few more speakers when suddenly closure was dropped upon us, and of course second reading was extended by the time necessary for debating the closure motion. To my complete surprise on the important part of the bill, discussion in committee of the whole, when it was clear that members of the opposition were
Income Tax
seriously concerned about several matters of great import to their constituencies and the whole country, closure was again imposed.
To give an example, Mr. Speaker, one of the subjects on which I did not contribute, but which engaged the attention of many members on this side, was insulation. Perhaps in no other country except the U.S.S.R. is insulation more important than in Canada. At no time in our history have fuel costs been so high and the subject of insulation so important. The government had obviously erred and was caught in a differential type of treatment for the people of Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island as compared with the rest of Canada. Instead of the minister admitting that the point had been well made and that he would do something to correct the situation, we debated it on and off for four or five weeks, and then the government surrendered outside the House in a meeting with provincial ministers.
My point is that if the government wants to govern, it must learn to recognize the feeling of the House and that discriminatory legislation cannot be put through without a long fight. My point is that closure is wrong, but when it is used it should be used with some sort of judgment and assessment. The House does not like closure, and unless there are matters of great national emergency it should never even be considered. The wrong place to apply closure is on the mundane things of tax law.
This budget did see some tax changes. I think it could be agreed now by all sides that the handling of the insulation program by the government was a failure, and it was made very clear in the debate.
Discussion of other points by hon. members should have been allowed, but this was not possible. We were cut off due to time allocation and closure. In particular, I felt the registered home owner savings plan was a good idea when it was brought in some three years ago. It encouraged the individual to save toward something necessary. The vast majority of people in Canada want to own their own homes. This program was cut off by the government without any consideration given to the tax liabilities of the poor devil who was encouraged to enter the program.
All of us, on both sides of the House, have many cases on file. I cite the example of a clergyman who does not receive much money by the very nature of his calling, who is provided with a free manse-as they call it-and who intends to retire in twelve years. He puts his money aside, a few hundred dollars a year into a registered home ownership savings plan, reduces his tax, and is pleased with the program. It means that down the road when he does retire, without a great pension, he will have a start toward purchasing his new home or the furniture therein. But suddenly it is announced that the program is cancelled. He has the alternative now of taking all that money back this year and paying full tax on it. He does not have the alternative of spreading it out, except if he buys an annuity, which does not meet his needs.

December 12, 1977
Income Tax
That is merely an example of the type of things that we, as members of parliament, should be debating, bringing the effect of tax law on individuals in Canada before the minister and before parliament. If I have a dozen examples, I would assume that every other member on each side of the House has an equal number. We cannot all participate in these debates. However, if just a few people had put their views forward, perhaps the minister would have been receptive and a change would have been made before the end of the year. This could have been done if there was a good mood in the House. You can only have a good mood in the House when it is obvious that the government is receptive to a positive, constructive idea.
The member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) dealt with the subject of the social insurance number. We know from personal conversations with the minister that he was as deeply shocked as we were that the civil servants in the Department of Finance and the Bank of Canada would deliberately break a solemn promise of a former Prime Minister made on the floor of this House. The Minister knew that was wrong. He knew the people of Canada did not want this closing in of regulations and controls, and for them to be known after a few years as only a number, not as persons any more. The majority of people in this country, and all members of parliament know I am right. We know that the member for Edmonton West is right. We are only expressing truth. The late Prime Minister Pearson gave his solemn word that this would not be applied to income tax.
When the Minister gave his answer to our proposals in the House that this should be eliminated, he was very impressed with the arguments of the member for Edmonton West, of myself and of one or two others. But then he said, "The civil servants have have told me that it has been on the income tax form since 1966. Therefore, apparently, it is the law of the Medes and the Persians-it cannot be changed. God has spoken! I am simply saying that one wrong in 1966 in breaking that pledge of the Prime Minister made in 1964, does not make it right now-to break it again for the second time.
This is not only with respect to bond coupons. You find out in many places throughout the country that they are demanding social insurance numbers. I am saying to the minister and to the Liberal government: you know that I am right, you know the people of Canada are right. There is not a single solitary argument to support the requirement for giving a SIN number when you buy a Canada Savings Bond. The only argument advanced on the positive side is that if a bond is lost, it will be easier to trace. Do you take away the civil liberties and freedom of 20 million individuals on the argument that you might save or find a lost bond-like a lost $10 bill? It does not hold. Then we have the ministers statement that since the SIN number is on the income tax form since 1966, he could not do much about it today, and so it is an accepted part of the law of the land. In the debate concerning this issue that will continued across the country for the next eight to ten months, the government will be on the defensive, trying to argue itself out of this position on the SIN number.

The government stands condemend of allowing the civil servants of Canada to change a promise of a Prime Minister and to contravene the wishes of parliament by applying the SIN number to everything. Until the government is willing to stand up to these termites who eat away at our freedom, then that government does not deserve to sit in office, and has to go. Ten years, even one hundred years from now the reduction and loss of our freedom will be more important than the mistakes made on the tax side of this particular budget.
We have endured bad taxes for years, and will continue to endure them. But we do not want to have to endure restriction on our liberties. The hon. member for Edmonton West should be congratulated because he was the only member who spotted this when the bill went through last March or April. I certainly take full blame for the fact that I missed it. When I did find out, I did what I could in a constructive way to ask the government to get rid of this silly SIN number on things that are not necessary.
Closure has prevented me from discussing this fascinating principle of the roll-over of capital gains on property. There is certainly no justice in what the government has done in suggesting it apply to farms and suggesting it apply to small business because these forms of private enterprise, these people as a rule do not receive much money during their working years. A small businessman who owns a store, a farmer who owns his farm, from the records we can show that he receives an average income well below that of the working class, and well below what people should be getting for the tremendous investment that they have at the present time. It may interest the House to know that in 1975 the average income of a farmer across Canada was approximately $8,000 per farm. This year, 1977, with the figures in for the first ten months, the average farmer will end up with approximately $4,000 a year. This does not include any reward or return on his interest, labour or management. It is simply the amount of money he will have after he has paid his expenses from his gross income.
This is at a time when labour is going up 6, 8, 10 or 12 per cent a year, and that is a restraint. Government costs are going up about the same level. However, for one important segment of our income earners, the agricultural sector, and equally important to miners, there has been a reduction of 50 per cent of their net income in a two-year period from $8,000 to $4,000.
This question of roll-over should have been discussed as part of an attempt by the government to make it a little more fair for this chap. When he finally comes to the end of his work period, he should have a chance to roll his enterprise over and move into a similar type operation without having to pay a tax on the move.
I did not get the opportunity during the committee of the whole to ask why this principle of roll-over is not applied to ownership in the form of shares. We, as a national objective,
December 12, 1977

should be trying in parliament to do everything we can to get Canadian as individuals to own their own country.
Our tax laws discriminate against Canadians owning shares in companies in their own country. That is why we in this country, in major segments of our economy own such a small proportion of the shares of large international companies. Our tax laws discriminate against it. We double tax any person who goes into ownership in the form of shares. We are not going to double tax them under this principle of roll over if they buy in the form of land or property.
We have moved a little bit on shares in the legislation where we have agreed to give privileges to the person who gets options. However, this privilege of being able to be treated differently on options under this legislation, Bill C-11, only applies to a person who gets options in a Canadian-owned private company. Why could this principle not be applied to the foreign-owned private company?
Many Canadians find that the only way they can be rewarded for doing something in Canada or abroad is to take their reward in the form of shares. They not only get their reward in the form of wages, but in the form of shares. But the first thing that happens when a company begins to make money is that they buy out the Canadians. There is usually a by-law of the company, as a type of protection, that you sell back to the company you have joined.
Usually these companies are foreign owned. If they are in newly developing nations, they cannot pay a Canadian very much money for his know-how to make things work so they give him a share interest. If his ideas are good, and the majority of shares are owned by the nationals of that country, the minute the company does well and share dividends on shares are going to be paid, they think of how they can buy you out. When things are going well, they want the dividends to stay in their own country. One can understand that reasoning because we have it here in Canada.
I suggest, as a constructive type of proposal, that we should allow this concept of roll over of capital gains to extend to all forms of property. The accepted philosophy is to make it possible to tax a person when money is taken into income, but when rolling over from one form of property to a similar type of property, the roll-over principle should be allowed to cover all forms of property ownership.
The minister did not respond to the second proposal I made. I hope his staff, including the parliamentary secretary, will bring this proposal to him. These proposals were made for the simple purpose of directing to a new minister, who is not responsible for most of this bill, some ideas to make this a better bill. It is the duty of every member of parliament in the House, including the opposition, to put forward proposals.
Our party voted for this legislation on second reading with the understanding that when it would go into committee of the whole we could put forward proposals to be included in the legislation. We found out, through inexperience maybe, and through a philosophy present on the other side of the House, that they do not want to accept proposals from the opposition.
Income Tax
I still hope they will learn to be democratic and learn that parliament is a place for talking.
Parliament is a place where you can put forward ideas in the hope that occasionally they may be a accepted. I am going to continue that policy of putting ideas forward. However, with the way this bill has been handled, with no sign of compromise and no sign of willingness to accept positive ideas, it is very difficult to keep up this belief.
Another subject that was not discussed in this legislation but should have been was the Turner budget of 1974. This budget we have now and this tax legislation are part of a series of continuing bits of tax law which all add up to disaster in Canada. I suppose everyone looked at the headline in this morning's Globe and Mail. I will read it to the House so that it will show on the record. It reads:
PM lost fiscal gamble; Canada pays with ailing economy
Then follows a fairly substantive analysis of all the mistakes the government has made since 1973 when Turner was the finance minister. The hon. member for Rosedale (Mr. Macdonald) was not able to change this drift and resigned from the portfolio. We see the very well-liked member from Shawini-gan, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien), coming into the position with great enthusiasm that he might be able to turn it around and end this drift of blunders that have been consistently the same since 1973. They have put Canada, a very strong country, having the products that the world wants and having every reason to be going at full blast, into a position where it has lost four years. We have not only been in recession but in stagflation throughout the whole period.
The key phrase that has to be remembered about the Turner budget of the spring of 1974, and repeated again in the fall of 1974, is that it applied double taxation to the resource industries of Canada. That budget of 1974 said to the provinces which owned the resources, "You have gone too far. You have been too greedy in raising your taxes three or four times on the resource industries. We are going to get back at you by doubling the penalty on these resource industries and not making those provincial taxes deductible."
Today in several of our provinces, with the provincial governments having doubled and quadrupled their tax level and the federal government not making the provincial taxes deductible, we have tax liability of 85 per cent to over 100 per cent.
As you look at the mines, they are going down. It is not just the big Inco, Falconbridge and Cominco mines. It is the small Canadian mines which are only producing $100 million worth of stuff a year, pretty small I admit. Craigmont is closing down. It is running out of high grade ore. Gibraltar is closing off. Most people in Canada have not heard of these mines. Nothing was more successful than Gibraltar until Turner's budget came in 1974. I am simply pointing out the obvious. It is not only the 4,000 miners in Ontario, but the miners in every province in Canada-they are going down the drain in a fast slide because of the double taxation imposed in this country in 1974. No attempt has been made in the bill
1776

December 12, 1977
Income Tax
before us to deal with this vitally important issue. So here we have a nation which should be strong, walking along on crutches.
Things are so bad that even the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) has realized he cannot fool the people any longer talking about unity when the policies of his own government are dragging a powerful country to its knees. Here is a mining industry, the most efficient in the world, with the ore the world needed, forced to its knees, going bankrupt, going out of business. Yet all we are talking about in this House is what kind of temporary, stop-gap measure we can devise to keep the workers employed for a few weeks longer or induce them to share what work there is.
The answer is simple. Tax law is competitive law, and if our tax laws are more severe than those of our competitors the industries which suffer from them will go out of business. Canada does not have a monopoly in world markets.
The budgets of the last couple of years have been bad budgets because they have failed to deal with the great mix-take which was made in 1974, the mistake of imposing double taxation. That mistake arose, naturally, from the philosophy of the government and the mandarins who advise it. Events have shown that it was not to the benefit of the mining industry, and now the administration must face the fact that the tax flowing into the treasury is being reduced rather than the contrary.
The only way in which a government which is bringing this country to its knees can win salvation under these circumstances is by admitting that it made a colosal blunder in 1974, changing its philosophy, and ending double taxation. This means letting the provinces keep what they have; let their tax be non-deductible, and then approach the provinces with the argument that, in line with the action taken federally, they ought to cut their own taxes closer to the 50 per cent level than to the 60 to 100 per cent level which prevails today.
In my opening remarks on second reading I spoke directly to the minister in connection with the theory of potential budgeting. I pointed out that the Economic Council of Canada has already mildly recommended that we move in this direction. I pointed out further that potential budgeting would only work during periods of slack employment and unused plant capacity. These two conditions have now made potential budgeting possible.
Potential budgeting consists simply of making tax reductions applicable to things which are not being done and which the nation wants to see done. This process helps the minister to balance his budget because he is not spending money. Let me give an example-there is only one example, to my knowledge, in the whole world, namely, the experience of the United States in 1964 when a young president, soon to be assassinated, accepted the concept, brand new as it was, and dropped the budget level by $10 billion. Everyone expected there would be a deficit at the end of the year of an additional $10 billion. But because tax reductions were applied to things the country

wanted, and because additional productive capacity was put into existence, government revenues increased; instead of going down by $10 billion the treasury ended up with an extra $19 billion. This was how the American Republic was pulled out of the slump and placed on a rising cycle which lasted until 1968.
I gave that example to the new Minister of Finance and, after talking to him later, I sent him a letter in which I put these ideas on record so that he could make use of them if he wished. To make sure that no one will think this is a secret matter between myself and the Minister of Finance I propose to take the time of the House, in closing, to put those observations formally before the chamber.
Following up my budget proposals in my speech of November 17, 1977, I submit the following paper at the request of your parliamentary secretary.
At this particular moment Canada's interests require a dramatic incentive for individuals to move towards some form of solar assisted energy savings. This need fits in with the opportunity for potential budgeting.
In almost every case solar hardware is capital intensive. In other words, one large capital investment now versus the usual 20 years of annual energy bills.
My proposal is that any type of capital expenditure to reduce utilization by the individual of traditional energy sources should be given the same tax treatment that business gets, namely:
(a)	100% write-off for proven hardware
(b)	150% write-off for hardware still in experimental stages (See Income Tax
Provision 1959-1971).
Then I listed the cases where the hardware has been proven and should be eligible for the 100 per cent write-off. Later, I listed 11 cases of experimental types of hardware which are still unproven. I will mention the 11 items on that list because they are the ones to which the House should pay attention. First, heat pumps. The reliability of heat pumps, whether air sourced or water sourced, has yet to be proven. Then there are the concentrator collectors for solar thermal energy conversion, commonly known as STEC.
The rest of the list reads as follows: heat storage facilities, methane production, vertical axis windmills, solar absorption air conditioning, residential photovoltaics, individual water recycling and conversion of waste to energy, conversion of cow manure to protein, energy plantation and the production of hydrogen. This is a first draft list of items which are within the performance capability of individuals and within reasonable economic parameters-I quote my source for that statement. Finally, 1 said to the minister:
What we are talking about in terms of national energy demand is small in percentage but important in dollars. Windpower, by 2000 A.D., could provide between one per cent and 5 per cent of our total national energy needs. Solar assisted heating of homes and water could by 2,000 A.D. provide between 10 and 15 per cent of our total national needs. Ten per cent of our national energy requirements would cost several billion dollars by 2,000 A.D.
In making these positive proposals 1 am trying to inject into this debate a constructive idea as to the way in which the minister could balance his budget without going further into deficit. I am proposing incentives in favour of the individual who takes the risk of developing techniques which have been carried out in the laboratory but which still remain to be proven by actual experience in a northern climate. Most of these things have been done in Canada, but still are not proven. Canada should move swiftly into using renewable
December 12, 1977

energy forms in replacement of the non-renewable forms which are being used at the present time.
What will happen from 1985 to 2000 if we continue to drift along utilizing oil, gas, and coal for our energy? Everyone in North America is dependent on those three forms. The cost will rise far beyond what it is today. It will put the United States and Canada into a tremendous deficit position in their international accounts. We are aware of what that means to our balance of payments position and inflation in our country. The danger should be clear from these figures.
Parliament should back the individual who is willing to take a risk providing things in the energy field. His proportion of the total energy field runs to approximately 15 per cent to 20 per cent. What we are doing is no more than what has been done for business. When business invests money in order to make money, that is tax deductible. That same principle should apply to the individual, if he spends money to reduce the amount of oil and gas necessary to heat his home, heat his water, and operate his car.
Our scientists and engineers have produced the ideas, but they are not allowed to go out and sell them. The knowledge contained in the laboratory report must be translated into an object which works, and that object has to be proven. In order to help the minister balance his budget, in order to alleviate the danger ahead as far as our balance of payments is concerned, and in an attempt to help the individual reduce his costs, 1 put these ideas forward.
We have not distinguished ourselves in the last two stages of this bill, on second reading and committee stage, because closure was used twice. 1 hope that these ideas will be accepted by the minister, the parliamentary secretary and those who make decisions. Then they can tell the mandarins in the Department of Finance and the Bank of Canada that these things will be incorporated into the next budget.
I am too late to save this bill because of the attitude of the government at the present time. We will have another budget in two or three months. Perhaps some of the constructive ideas regarding insulation, roll-over, and capital gains can be implemented. This is what parliament is for: we must be allowed to help the government get this country moving, balance its budget, and at the same time help Canadians. If that is the case, some of the dignity and usefulness will be restored to this place.
Some day a minister of finance will come into this House and realize that for the last 30 years every minister of finance has been under the thumbs of the financial advisers of the government. These financial advisers can be dedicated, sincere, and charming, but they do not know what they are doing. They have been consistently wrong for 30 years. This is a year of miracles, because economists are beginning to admit that they do not know what is wrong. The public servants who advise the Minister of Finance have not faced up to this truth. Perhaps it would not hurt to see a minister of finance applying
Adjournment Motion
ordinary common sense and a theory slightly different from the one used at present.
I reminded the Minister of Finance that he came from Shawinigan. Surely a person with common sense from Shawinigan has an obligation not to follow the sheep who come from the big city, because they are only taught to obey orders. Canadians would like to see some common sense from Shawinigan. The minister should take over the Department of Finance and be reasonable about some of these changes, not to mention the fact that parliament should operate in a slightly more democratic manner.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) and the hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain (Mr. Hamilton) have dealt extensively with the matter of the government using closure on this bill. 1 had intended to speak to that point at some length, but I will not, since they have covered it so expertly.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext: Do you feel the same way?

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
I feel the same way as my colleagues, because it is a regressive step for the government to use closure at any time. It was particularly regressive in this instance, because we were beginning to get into the nub of the bill. The government has brought in several amendments, and 1 am sure many more would have come to light had the debate continued.
May I call it five o'clock, Mr. Speaker?

speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should set up a special subcommittee of the Standing Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs, to investigate and report on the needs of Canada's physically and mentally handicapped citizens; in order to provide a basis of information, [Mr. Deputy Speaker.)
necessary in avoiding the current costly duplication and overlapping of services, and essential in planning legislation for a comprehensive program of services at the federal, provincial and municipal levels of government to support and supplement the excellent work of voluntary organizations; all with a view to making it possible for the handicapped to live a creative, fruitful and independent life in the family and community, and thereby placing Canada in a position of leadership in the rehabilitation movement in preparation for the XIV World Congress of Rehabilitation International to be held in Winnipeg during June 1980.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I think this is about the fourth occasion in the pre-Christmas season that I have had the privilege of bringing in this motion, or a similar motion, before the House of Commons.
I would like to say right at the outset that last year, as an indication of the fact that this motion is basically humanitarian and has no partisan overtones, the hon. member for York South (Mrs. Appolloni) seconded the motion. I am sure the hon. lady is still in sympathy with its purpose. This year I would be very happy if the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) would second the motion, because again I want to indicate that it is bi-partisan in all respects and also because this is the year that the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre has been specially honoured in the House because of his long years of service. 1 might also say that he is a representative of the geriatric sector of the population which is becoming one of the largest segments of the population in percentage terms, standing at about 10 per cent and increasing fast.

subsubtopic: SUGGESTION SPECIAL SUB COMMITTEE INVESTIGATE NEEDS OF HANDICAPPED CITIZENS
speechtext: Also the wisest segment.

subsubtopic: SUGGESTION SPECIAL SUB COMMITTEE INVESTIGATE NEEDS OF HANDICAPPED CITIZENS
speechtext:
The resolution that is before the House this afternoon affects very directly the problems of our senior citizens. The reason I like to have it debated in December is that in the Christmas season we are always more responsive and sensitive to humanitarian issues.
Every hon. member is aware of the fact that one of the most popular persons in the rehabilitation movement is Tiny Tim. He represents the large number of children with handicaps. He himself comes from amongst their number and represents them in that successful fund raising program known as the Easter Seal Campaign.
Tiny Tim is associated intimately with Christmas in that famous Christmas story of Scrooge who, in the midst of Christmas activities many years ago, had a change of heart and Scrooge the hard-hearted, turned out to be Scrooge the humanitarian. I hope against hope that this afternoon any reservations that the government might have had in the past with respect to approving this motion will dissolve in the warmth of the Christmas spirit and that today we will be able to obtain unanimous consent for this motion.

December 12, 1977

It is a very simple motion proposing the setting up of a subcommittee of the Standing Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs to give consideration to the needs of Canada's handicapped population in preparation for the World Congress which will be held in Winnipeg in 1980.
Last year we came within a hair's breadth of having this motion approved. The speakers who took part in the debate at that time all indicated that they were strongly in support of the motion, and the one deterrent was expressed by the hon. member for Fort William (Mr. McRae), who was then parliamentary secretary to the minister of national health and welfare, in the following words:
Mr. Speaker, the motion is an excellent one. I have only one reason for not accepting it at this point. It could have been accepted much earlier. However, we are now only a matter of weeks away from a new social services bill being dealt with in this House.
The handicapped in this country have been studied a great deal. It is now time for action. The bill to be introduced is an action bill. Action for the handicapped in this area will come sooner if we follow the normal procedure rather than setting up this subcommittee.
We know now that action has been deferred. I am not going to harp on that theme this afternoon, but the legislation has disappeared from the order paper. There is a promise in the Speech from the Throne that it will be resurrected.
I believe that in anticipation of this important congress in Winnipeg in 1980 we should get on with the very important business of gathering together all the data that is available so that we will have a comprehensive picture of the rehabilitation situation in this country in time for Canada to host that important congress adequately.
1 have the assurance-perhaps that will help the government in making up its mind on this matter-from the government House leader that he sees no impediment to establishing a subcommittee of that kind. Perhaps I should read that assurance from the hon. gentleman into the record again:
As you know, the government will be introducing legislation during this session on the subject of social services, including rehabilitation of the disabled. This bill, after second reading, will be referred to the Standing Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs where witnesses may be called and every facet of the bill considered. I do not think that anyone would object to the kind of work to which you refer being done at that time, perhaps by a subcommittee.
As 1 have indicated, the circumstances have changed from last year with respect to the legislation. That is largely because the funding formula has been changed, and it will be necessary to renegotiate the changed formula with the provincial governments, which have ultimate responsibility for the implementation of any legislation of this kind.
The hon. member for Toronto-Lakeshore, who is now the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Robinson), and who is with us today, indicated in his statement last year that he was in favour of the resolution as it appears on the order paper today. His only concern was that it be integrated with the proposed legislation. I trust that he will continue his support of the resolution today and also see to it that it gets consensus, because I think it is absolutely essential to have the reassurance that Canada was
Handicapped Citizens
in earnest when it extended its invitation at the World Congress of Rehabilitation in Tel Aviv in 1976 to host the next congress in 1980. We are one year closer to that congress. There are only two years left. The congress will involve 7,000 people from all countries of the world, and it will consider in depth the problems of rehabilitation of the handicapped in all their aspects, including physical and mental handicaps.
There will be a series of seminars in all major centres in the week preceding the congress, which will have a major input in the expansion of knowledge in this field because only the professionals will be involved in the seminars. These will be the various professionals involved in the rehabilitation movement: physiatrists, doctors of physical medicine, social workers, occupational therapists, physiotherapists, psychologists, and other specialists in the field of human relations. There is going to be a post-conference series of seminars throughout North America, so I think hon. members can see that there will be a major breakthrough in the rehabilitation movement.
As I have intimated, the debate last year indicated that there was a misunderstanding of what we are trying to do. We do not want this subcommittee to be set up as a fact finding committee because there is much information available in Canada. It is an attempt to bring it all together. There are at least 48 volunteer agencies which are doing an outstanding job in the field of rehabilitation, but governments have not become too intimately involved in the process up to the present time.
There are rehabilitation centres in every major community of Canada. Recently Nova Scotia opened an excellent rehabilitation facility. A seminar was conducted there under the auspices of the Canadian Rehabilitation Council for the Disabled. A new organization known as COPOH, the Committee of Provincial Organizations on the Handicapped, has just come into being. An executive director has been appointed. He is a well known leader in the field, Mr. Wilf Race. He has worked for the government in several capacities with respect to handicapped citizens. He is handicapped himself, and he will carry the responsibility for the input of physically handicapped citizens in the rehabilitation movement itself. There are outstanding leaders of international repute. 1 previously mentioned Dr. Gustave Gingras.
Canada has been accepted as the host country for 1980 because of our outstanding reputation in this respect. We are not trying to indulge in a fact-finding operation. We want to bring all the facts together in a formal report so that it will be available to the people who visit Canada in 1980. There is an upsurge of interest in Canada and all over the world in the problems of the handicapped. The desire for independent living is being expressed at the present time all over the world.
Last week I attended a debate at the United Nations Third Committee where I was asked to make a statement on behalf of Canada with regard to a resolution which very closely parallels the resolution we have before the House today. Canada is a co-sponsor of that resolution, and its intent is to establish an advisory committee-that is the intent of my

December 12, 1977
Handicapped Citizens
resolution here-which will sponsor the Year of Rehabilitation which is scheduled to commence in 1981. This will flow out of the congress which will be held in Canada in 1980, so hon. members can see that the two go hand in hand.
Let me quote briefly a short excerpt from the statement I made last Thursday afternoon in the United Nations Third Committee as follows:
We view the Committee's primary task as that of promoting greater public awareness of the disabled and the problems with which they must cope. For too long they have been ignored by the community or thrust onto the sidelines with a pension and a shrug. There has been the usual discrimination that kept the handicapped people out of sight and out of mind, hidden away in institutions that were little better than human warehouses. Most severely disabled people died at an early age. Those who survived and made it did so through exceptional ability, family resources, hard work or just plain luck.
Then I went on to congratulate the international community for becoming involved in this process. I am sure hon. members will be pleased to know that the resolution passed unanimously-by consensus, as they say-in the United Nations body. Canada was a co-sponsor and took an active part in the debate. It was supported by a series of other countries, and I will name just a few: Algeria, Argentina, Belgium, Canada, Costa Rica, Cuba, Democratic Yemen, Egypt, Finland, Federal Republic of Germany, Greece, India, The Philippines, the United States of America, Yugoslavia, and so forth. This resolution was unanimously supported.
The congress will be much more significant in terms of humanitarian causes sponsored in Canada than was the Habitat Conference in Vancouver. We hope that the federal government will give the same financial support to the Rehabilitation Congress as it did to the Habitat Conference because I am sure the results will be much more positive.
In closing let me give some of the priorities, as I see them, as we prepare for the 1980 congress. It is imperative that the new social service legislation be in operation. I picked up a publication at the United Nations last week entitled "Recent Trends in Legislation Concerning Rehabilitation Services for Disabled Persons in Selected Countries." Unfortunately, Canada is not included in this presentation. I think it is important that Canada proceed as quickly as possible with its social service legislation so that we might be in the forefront of leadership in this regard.
The second priority we should establish is an advisory committee to keep the government abreast of developments in the field of rehabilitation in anticipation of the 1980 congress. Advisory committees should be operating at the provincial level as well, and the province of Ontario has already set up such an advisory committee.
The third priority is to provide funds for a resource and information centre. We have all this information and we have all sorts of expertise. We have outstanding leadership as well, but it all needs to be brought together so that it can be readily available for the 6,000 or 7,000 people who will come to Canada looking for leadership in two and a half years. The

Department of National Health and Welfare has already sponsored a study through the Chedoke Institute at McMas-ter, establishing the need for a resource and information centre. It must now assist the Canadian Rehabilitation Council for the Disabled in setting up such a centre.
Fourth, the government should provide funds for a coordinator to assist the Canadian Council for the Disabled in organizing the congress. It will be largely a congress of voluntary agencies supported by the federal government, the provincial government, and the municipal government of Winnipeg. This means it will be people talking to people rather than governments talking to governments, and with this sort of dialogue I think we can achieve positive results.
Finally, we should have a subcommittee of the Standing Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs bring in a report on much the same basis as the excellent report brought down by the subcommittee that dealt with the problems in Canada's penal system, operating as a subcommittee of the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs.
These are all positive recommendations, Mr. Speaker. I do not want to speak at great length, and I wish to allow other members an opportunity to take part. I hope we will get a consensus for this resolution in the Canadian parliament on the same basis as we achieved unanimous support last Thursday at the United Nations.
