Mr. Speaker, I should like to indicate once again my wholehearted support of the motion presented by the hon. member for Brandon-Souris (Mr. Dinsdale). I also want to commend him for the persistence with which he pleads in this House the rights and needs of our disabled people.
The hon. member made some reference to the years that some of us have been here. I believe he is a member of that club himself. In years of service he is about No. 3. There is an advantage to being in this club of members with longevity in that one realizes if he sticks with an issue that is right and just, sooner or later it will be achieved. It is tragic that so many of these issues are won later rather than sooner, but if we have to cope with a government that moves slowly it is a good thing that there are members who stick with an issue until it is won.
I hope today may be the day when the effort of the hon. member for Brandon-Souris (Mr. Dinsdale) is rewarded and this House agrees to the motion which simply states that, in the view of the House, the government should arrange for the appointment of the subcommittee to which the hon. member has referred.
It seems to me that to take that position, especially in view of the international congress that is to be held in Winnipeg in 1980, is an important gesture in showing our increased concern for the rights and needs of our disabled people. It is as recent

December 12, 1977

as during the days when Mr. St. Laurent was Prime Minister that the first disabled persons' act was put on the statute books of this country. There was, of course, a blind persons' act many years ago, but the fact is that we have been slow to recognize the rights of this particular group of people at the federal level. We all subscribe to the theory that there should be more equality of opportunity in our society. We tend to think of that in terms of the greater equalization of incomes of people, but it seems to me this is an area where something more than money is required.
Persons with handicaps or disabilities, start the race of life on unequal terms. They deserve not just sympathy or adequate compensation but every possible opportunity for rehabilitation and training so that they can have a life as nearly normal as possible. I think it is fair to say, as has been said by so many people, that civilization is judged very largely by what it does for those who are old or young or handicapped or disabled in various ways. We have made some strides in this direction in this country but they have been too few and are terribly disjointed. Not long ago the Canadian Council on Social Welfare published a volume entitled On Again Off Again, or something like that, about the disjointed nature of the services and legislation for our disabled people.
1 do not want to take the time of the Elouse because I should like to see the motion considered and passed, not just given the usual treatment of being talked out. I am pleased that the hon. member for Brandon-Souris brought this forward again. I think this House owes it to the disabled people of Canada and to Canada's good name to get more active in this field than we have been to this point. For that reason I hope the House will agree to pass this motion this afternoon.

speakeroldname: Mr. W. Kenneth Robinson (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
subsubtopic: SUGGESTION SPECIAL SUB COMMITTEE INVESTIGATE NEEDS OF HANDICAPPED CITIZENS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at the outset I would like to congratulate the hon. member for Brandon-Souris (Mr. Dinsdale) for bringing this very important matter before the House. He has done it before and has shown a great deal of persistence, and he should be congratulated for his persistence as well. I believe the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) pointed that out quite adequately. I would also like to congratulate him on the recommendations that he has suggested in his remarks, which I am sure will be considered very carefully by the government when this whole matter is being considered. Whilst I am handing out accolades, I should mention the tie he is wearing today, which I understand has emblazoned on it a wheelchair, being the symbol for disabled people generally. He is to be commended too for this outward manifestation of his feeling for people who are disabled in this country.
Mr. Speaker, it is with great pleasure that I speak on this motion today because I feel that the government has accomplished much in the field of services for the disabled to date. However, as the country is evolving, the services should also expand to serve a larger target group. Society would benefit more if it could give to all of its members a better quality of life that would lead them to become more independent, to participate in industry and society according to their abilities.
Those considered physically handicapped represent a sizeable 10 per cent of the population, and yet, whenever normalization and integration of this group is discussed, two kinds of barriers are mentioned with respect to the physically handicapped, architectural barriers and attitudinal barriers; and for the mentally and socially handicapped, attitudinal barriers. According to a number of professionals in the rehabilitation field, it is really a toss-up as to which kind of barrier is the most important cause preventing the handicapped from full participation in community life. Many of them, in fact, are convinced that attitudinal barriers are the most pervasive kind of negativism. They feel that eradication of these should be a first priority.
In connection with attitudinal barriers facing the handicapped, a Canadian researcher, A. Ruth Hilland, in an article published in Rehabilitation Digest of February 1975, suggests that the roots of this prejudice lie in the fact that society values people because they have social standing, wealth, beauty, are active, useful, productive and efficient. When such criteria are applied to the handicapped it is surprising that they are devalued. She feels that before our attitudes with

December 12, 1977
Handicapped Citizens
respect to the handicapped can be changed, society's values must be changed. I quote from her statement as follows:
And should it not be possible for differences not to lessen a person's worth, not to mean that he should be treated as 'less than human'? A change in attitude on the part of the non-disabled will come about through increased exposure to the disabled.
She stresses that the exposure should be "normal". In other words, people must see the handicapped every day in normal situations; in the classroom, in ordinary jobs, housing, neighbourhood, clubs, communities, using ordinary transportation and so on. Entertainment channels, she feels, are also a good source of depicting the physically unattractive as esteemed, valued and respected, such as the television serial we have all become acquainted with entitled "Ironside".
The handicapped have always wanted, and are now demanding, respect of their basic rights: the right to rehabilitation, the right to work, and the right to be integrated into society. The handicapped person needs others to understand and to truly realize that he is a person like any other with the same requirement to love and to be loved, to work and enjoy himself, and the ability to overcome his handicap if he is given the necessary technical aids. The sentiment is strongly reinforced by a comment made by Jacques Couillard, the Director of Social Rehabilitation at the Quebec Workers' Compensation Board, and I quote:
Each time that we put the handicapped apart, each time that we treat him differently, we do not help the way he views himself nor the way the public views him . .. instead we make his job of integrating himself into society even more difficult.
This statement is most real to those handicapped individuals confined to institutions, most often homes for the retarded, the aged, or the chronically ill. Granted, they are treated, housed and fed, but nothing else. Is it any wonder, then, that an alderman who lived in an institution in Thunder Bay was first in line for a place in a "group home", an alternative concept in housing, preferable by far to these disabled individuals who do not require nursing care. The disabled want and are entitled to live with dignity and as independently as possible. But more adequate housing fulfils only part of the need; it is also necessary to provide these persons with the services required to live independently. They might include the following:
1.	Attendant care to permit a disabled person to perform such activities as dressing and bathing.
2.	Day care services for those who work and have family responsibilities.
3.	Homemaker services.
4.	Meals on wheels.
5.	Recreation services.
6.	Adequate transportation services.
7.	Access to all community services and employment.
It is possible for the provinces, at the present time, to provide a number of these services through the Canada Assistance Plan, in particular, day care services, homemaker services, and meals on wheels, when the recipient is a person in need. The disabled, however, are also quick to remind govern-

ments that programs in Sweden, for instance, indicate that it often costs less to provide a person with the services necessary to make him independent than it does to maintain him in an institution. For example, when our older population experience difficulty in keeping their homes going, they frequently have no choice but to move into an institution where they could be separated.
No institution can provide the warm, comfortable, normal day-to-day life we all become used to. Disruption of this pattern of life tends to destroy the life of older folks. There are more disadvantages. They have found that a lack of privacy is the worst thing about institutions, especially when it is combined with a feeling of solitude; life then becomes hardly worth living. This situation was portrayed vividly in a film from the National Film Board shown recently on French television and entitled "Au bout de mon age" by George Dufaux.
Many handicapped persons are looking forward to the day when they will be able to return to or join the labour market. Employment to the majority of the handicapped means a regular pay cheque and independence. They do not want special treatment; they want jobs that society accepts as valid work. In essence, the handicapped call for greater employment opportunities within a broader range of formats. They want a job and a chance to prove themselves; they also ask that their abilities and not their disabilities be stressed.
At the Employability of the Handicapped Conference held in Toronto in November 1976, one of the most frequent remarks was that employers in diverse trades and work situations found handicapped individuals to be among some of their best employees-dependable, honest, self-starting and hard working. Despite this well established fact, handicapped people still often find themselves hampered by the attitudes of personnel officers, the physical barriers in many work places, problems of transportation, and by a general lack of awareness of what they can do. Welfare rolls are swollen by handicapped persons who are far from being there by choice but yet have not been able to find any work. Estimates for reducing the welfare rolls paid for by our tax dollars through employment of handicapped individuals range as high as 40 per cent. Only a small segment of the physically handicapped is incapable of working. In a society as technologically advanced as ours, work is no longer defined in terms of physical labour.
The motion now before the House deals mainly with the needs of the physically handicapped. The mentally handicapped, the mentally retarted in particular, have the same need for community integration. Why confine them to expensive institutions and pay for their upkeep when they could be in the labour force earning their own living and or participating in their community's development? In 1967, the Department of National Health and Welfare authorized a special mental retardation fund of $2,500,000 to be allocated over five years to health and welfare research and demonstration projects. In addition, support for research has been made available under the public health research grant. The Canadian Association of Mental Retardation receives sustained assistance in the form of an annual operating grant from the
December 12, 1977

federal government and assistance from the provincial governments.
They will be studying, over a period of time, the actual operation of model systems of community services for the mentally retarded in order to arrive at sound decisions concerning the mechanisms and timing of transfer from institutional to communal living. Great interest has, I know, been aroused in the pilot program in Lethbridge, Alberta and its progress will, it is hoped, chart guidelines for the future development of services to the mentally handicapped in Canada.
With regard to employment, it is very unfortunate that a large percentage of retarded adults are embarrassed about working in sheltered workshops and are discouraged by the low status jobs they must do. Employment plays an important role in their life and contributes in many ways to self-confidence and self-esteem. The kind of training they receive often does not prepare them for a regular job. I am sure that there are many valuable and meaningful jobs retarded adults can do and should be encouraged to do. 1 strongly believe that we should establish proper training programs which will prepare and encourage them to undertake a rewarding job. Consider for a moment that mental retardation is one of the major handicapping conditions of childhood, and is one of the most common disabilities.
"The question of income maintenance", states a brief presented by the National Steering Committee of the Physically Disabled, "has been an issue of great concern to Canada's physically disabled population for decades". The advent of the Canada Pension Plan and the Canada Assistance Plan in the mid-sixties provided the disabled with income to meet their basic needs.
The disabled have pointed out, however, that their basic needs are not the same as those of the non-disabled and that, in fact, "any disability", as one of them said, "is a luxury I can ill afford". The same brief explains that the question of protecting a disabled person's income from the erosion of costs incurred as a direct result of the disability is as important as the income itself and has equal applicability to those in receipt of social allowances as it does to those who are able to provide for themselves. For example, many physically disabled person: are capable of accepting remunerative employment, but the costs of transportation to and from work, if the individual cannot use public transportation or buy his own car, may be so high as to make employment unprofitable.
To assess the impact of inexpensive, reliable transportation services for the disabled in terms of employability alone would be an impractical task, and to assess the impact of such a service on other areas of a handicapped person's life would be downright impossible. What I am saying is that this service is not a special favour to the handicapped but a necessity, a right.
As most hon. members are now aware, a block financing proposal has recently been made to the provinces to cover the
Handicapped Citizens
costs of social services including transportation services for the disabled. It represents the substituting of one financing arrangement, namely block funding, for another, the conditional shared cost arrangement associated with the new social services legislation, Bill C-57.
Under the block financing arrangement, the provinces will have more latitude in deciding upon those services which may be funded with the assistance of the federal contribution. It will be the prerogative of the provinces to establish the criteria for eligibility as well as for the specific needs identified within their respective communities.
In the event that the block financing approach is adopted, it will be made clear that one of the purposes of increased federal financing is to support the development and expansion of social services which respond more adequately to the needs of the mentally and physically handicapped and various other groups.
Canada's disabled are entitled to a more "normal", a more equal and a happier lot within our society. Adequate social services legislation is just one step toward achieving this goal.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to begin by thanking my friend, the hon. member for Cochrane (Mr. Stewart), for allowing me to take a moment of time that was designated to him to indicate my support and enthusiasm for the resolution.
I hope that if a subcommittee is set up and it embarks on this work, it will be very cautious about adopting ideologies with regard to treatment of the handicapped. Those of us who watch events taking place in the United States will be aware of a federal law recently passed which is in the process of implementation now. It is referred to in the trade by the nickname "mainstreaming".
Mainstreaming of the handicapped, particularly handicapped young people, involves removing them from institutions and putting them back into the general community schools. The theory is that in the general community they will learn to integrate better. They will avoid the isolation that comes from being educated and growing up only with the handicapped.
As much as this is an interesting idea, an idea that in the case of many, many handicapped people should be pursued, I want to warn the House and indicate to hon. members that it is extremely dangerous to move so rapidly from one ideology to another. Surveys and studies are indicating now that these institutions which are being abandoned have indeed worked very well for the majority of people who have gone through them.
As for the small minority which might be capable of "mainstreaming", the benefits to them might be outweighed by other factors, for example, the lack of the individual attention or

special consideration available to them in schools or institutions specifically set up to serve their needs.
I wish the hon. member well. I hope a committee of this sort could be launched to do the work he has in mind. I hope, too, that it will learn from the mistakes of the United States, that it will not swing from one ideology to another but adopt a middle course and be guided by the many years of experience, both good and bad, which are available to those dealing with the handicapped.

Mr. Speaker, as the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) so ably pointed out about a year ago in debate in this House:
One of the ways to measure a society is to see what it does for the less fortunate. The more we do for the disabled and the more we give them the chance to live normal, natural lives, the better is our society.
Access is the key toward promoting this normal, natural life for the disabled. Barrier-free environments benefit everyone. Studies of improved access to the University of Chicago showed that 80 per cent of non-disabled students chose to use the new entrances. Insurance companies report that buildings which have been made accessible to the handicapped by using non-skid surfaces, freely opening doors, suitable step dimensions, and so on, have shown a decreased accident rate for all users.
People in special categories are people who work, pay taxes, answer summonses, and are asked to contribute to voluntary organizations. Too often, however, they are not able to get into places of business, into the office where tax errors can be discussed, into the building where the traffic fine is to be paid, or into the church or "Y" where they would like to participate.
I have said nothing about the inaccessibility of places of education and employment. In view of these facts of life, is it any wonder that somewhat close to 40 per cent of the handicapped are unemployed-note, I did not say unemployable. That this figure is not higher is a credit to the determination, ingenuity and ambitions of those disabled individuals who continue to function in society in spite of the fact that at times it seems to be designed to frustrate and discourage them.
The latest available statistics show that the number of people age 20 to 64 injured in car accidents alone in Ontario increased from 54,053 in 1971 to 62,018 in 1975. This is an increase of approximately 12.5 per cent. Though there is no way of calculating how many were permanently handicapped, it can safely be assumed that a substantial number of these people have been disabled to the extent that they must now depend more on society for aid in the activities of daily living than they ever did before their injury. The enormity of this problem is put in more tangible perspective when you consider that one is seven people in this country cope daily with some form of handicap which significantly affects not only the style, but the quality of their lives.
It is not possible to calculate the number of lives that could be positively revitalized and the amount of potential that could be freed by simply making every building, every facility, and every area of a given community, accessible. Total and auto-
December 12, 1977

matic accessibility must be recognized as essential before the quality of life available to able bodied individuals can also be truly shared by the handicapped.
Some may say, "This is an ideal, a dream; that it is simply too expensive to consider the concept of total accessibility". Is it? In 1967 a cost study report in the United States conducted on a one-story building on a level site, a multi-story on a sloping site, and so on, showed a range of 0 to 2.5 per cent increase to accommodate the handicapped, with a saving in one case. The increase was less than 1 per cent unless an elevator had to be added.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as 1 was saying at five o'clock, one of the tragedies of this bill is not what is in the bill but what is missing. It is an act to amend the Income Tax Act, and it could have been used as a lever to get the economy moving. Whatever plan is brought forward by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) in the months ahead most assuredly will contain amendments to the Income Tax Act.
I was shocked to see in one of the major newspapers a headline referring to plant closings and lay-offs. We read more and more about inflation, plants closing, unemployment, increased trade deficits and a staggering balance of payments deficit. We had an inflation psychology before, and now we have the reverse of that in our economy today. People are reading and seeing so much about gloom in the economy that it affects decisions which should be made in conducting business. When one looks at manufacturing industries in Canada, particularly in Ontario and Quebec where the bulk of them are located, and when one looks at the trade deficits those companies face, which are estimated to amount to $11.5 billion by the end of this fiscal year, one realizes that industry is eroding.
In 69-70 the trade deficit in manufactured goods was approximately $1.5 billion. From 1972 the trade deficit increased to a point where it was better than $10 billion in
1976,	and unfortunately it is estimated to be $11.5 billion in
1977.	The budget should have had provisions which would be beneficial to the manufacturing trade, but there is little for them. There is a great deal of discussion about low productivity in Canada, but little in the bill to offset that.
Some people regard productivity as a matter of labour, but it is also capital availability, interest costs, energy costs, man-

agement expertise, labour talents, transportation costs, machinery efficiency and the kind and quality of research and development. All of these things play a part in productivity. The $11.5 billion deficit is directly connected with research and development in Canada.
Comparisons have been made between Canada and Japan, and Canada and Germany. In Japan in 1969-70, something in the order of 26 per cent of the GNP was spent on research and development, new plants and machinery. Today they are reaping the benefit of that decision and action. The investment tax benefit in Quebec is 7.5 per cent, in the Maritimes it is 10 per cent, and in the rest of Canada it is 5 per cent. When it is looked at closely, the investment tax credit for research and development is also subject to tax. It is like the insulation tax: the grant is given and then it is taken away. In this case the same thing is being done. The net income from the 5 per cent investment tax, when it is netted out, is approximately 2.5 per cent.
Once again we see the government dealing in sleight of hand taxation. It announces a tax incentive and then taxes that tax incentive. In the case of research and development, people will find that in practice they must deduct from their research and development the 5 per cent investment tax credit before they calculate their tax, and then they must deduct the investment tax credit from the tax payable. The net effect is that they get only half the rate the government says they will get. 1 say that is absolute fraud. Many decisions are going to be made by some people who will not look very closely into this or discuss it with their auditors. Many decisions are going to be made based on the fact that people will feel they are going to get 5 per cent, 7.5 per cent or 10 per cent investment tax benefits, but they will not. They will realize that when they make up their income tax returns next time around.
It is like the insulation grant. The government makes grants because of the energy crisis and comes along after and taxes part of those grants away. The problems facing Canada are real and deep, and the solutions should not be saved or stored for some appropriate political time. That is what is happening now.
The government could have put into Bill C-ll many measures which would have stopped the disastrous attitude which is being instilled and the doom which is abroad in the country today. The government could have stopped a good deal of that with a little bit of blue sky in the budget speech or in Bill C-ll, but it is not there; and judging from what we hear from the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien), the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and all others who speak on these matters, we cannot look forward to a tax cut, in spite of the recommendations of major organizations in this country such as the Economic Council of Canada, the Conference Board, the Canadian Chamber of Commerce and the Canadian Manufacturers' Association. All these organizations have recommended tax cuts at the sales tax level, at the corporate level and at the personal income tax level. Why has the government not done
{Mr. Kempling.]
this? We see the disaster which is upon us in the resource industries and the difficulty our mining industry is in right now. We are now beginning to feel the effects of the 1974 double taxation which was imposed by a former minister of finance, Mr. Turner, and much of our mining industry is in serious trouble today and will be in the future.
Where will employment be created? The government says that new employment initiatives have to come from industry. What is there for industry? There are no particular tax benefits. As I said, the research and development tax credit is a sham. It is only half of what the government says it is, when it is worked out. If industry is to be required to employ the unemployed in this country, it will need much more stimulation than that. That additional stimulation should have been in the budget. There should have been some stimulation for the manufacturing sector of our economy.
It is estimated that if our economy grows at an annual rate of 5.5 per cent, it will take something in the order of five years to bring our rate of unemployment down from its present 8.7 per cent to 7 per cent. There is a tremendous job to be done. At a time when our plants are operating at 80 per cent capacity the government introduces a bill to amend the Combines Investigation Act and has even suggested that the committee hearings on that legislation be limited. This is the wrong time to introduce that type of legislation. Every major economic body in Canada has suggested to the government that there be a major cut, particularly in sales tax and in personal income tax.
The submissions of the Economic Council of Canada, the Conference Board, the Canadian Chamber of Commerce and the Canadian Manufacturers' Association all agree that personal and business tax cuts are needed. They all agree that retail sales tax should be reduced and in some cases removed. They all agree that productivity must be improved if we are to compete in the marketplace in the months ahead.
To the business community the picture facing us is pretty dismal. We are not competitive in any of the minerals we are selling. We have seen what has happened in the nickel industry, and it is suggested that the copper and iron ore industry could be in as much trouble in the months ahead. We have some difficulties in the agricultural industry. They may right themselves, but they are there. Only a few years ago we controlled the world's nickel supply. We had about 95 per cent of it in our hands, and now that share is down to about 40 per cent.
In view of this situation I would have thought that the government would have used this last budget to do something about the double taxation on our minerals. Depending upon which province is involved, that taxation runs anywhere from 85 per cent to 100 per cent. In one province that taxation was over 100 per cent until the residents there saw to it that the government of the day was turned out. We face a tremendous balance of payments problem, and the amount of money that is going into investment in industry is shrinking each month. I wonder why the government contributes to organizations like the Economic Council of Canada and then does not heed its

December 12, 1977

recommendations. I read with a great deal of interest the 14th Annual Report of the Economic Council of Canada. One recommendation which is found at page 87 of the report is as follows:
We recommend that, over the next two fiscal years, the federal and provincial governments implement permanent personal income tax cuts that would increase the annual disposable incomes of consumers by a total of $2 billion in addition to reductions resulting from indexation.
At page 88 we find the following recommendation:
We recommend that provinces reduce their sales taxes by at least 1 percentage point on taxable consumer goods and services other than such items as gasoline, alcohol, and cigarettes.
Recommendation No. 4 at page 91 is as follows:
We recommend that the federal government, together with representative organizations, establish appropriate advisory and consultative mechanisms (with adequate staff resources) to examine serious long-term structural issues.
The following remarks are very appropriate and are as follows:
It is possible to move the economy back to a more desirable growth path, but this will require structural change as well as demand stimulation. Even with the initiatives that we are suggesting, unemployment rates will probably not fall below 7 per cent until after 1980. Inflation will persist roughly in line with the inflation rates of Canada's major trading partners. Without improvement in this country's capacity to control costs and improve productivity, we face the prospect of persistent overall government deficits, no improvement in current account balances, and rising foreign indebtedness. Neither federal nor provincial governments will have much flexibility for new expenditure programs. A concerted effort to improve the structure of the Canadian economy over the medium term is obviously needed.
They finally conclude:
The Council believes that Canadians and Canadian Institutes can cope with the challenges foreseen. This task will require a realistic assessment of problems; it will require imagination to perceive opportunities; it will require confidence to achieve change; and it will require greater trust and understanding among the different groups in the Canadian economy.
How true that is and how wise that group of people was to put those words into the report. The tragedy is that no one on the government side appears to be listening and the shame is that they do not seem to care.
1 know that some other of my colleagues want to contribute to this debate and I have said what I wanted to say. I am unhappy with the progress of this budget; I am unhappy with the fact that closure was imposed on the debate; 1 am unhappy that more was not done. There was plenty of time between the introduction of the budget last March and the introduction of this bill when many things could have been put into the ways and means motion, but the government saw fit to do less than nothing on it.
I am particularly unhappy that the minister has not seen fit to come forward with a concrete plan. In fact, he seems to be telegraphing to the community at large that nothing will be done about taxation; we will have the same level of taxation in the months ahead. He says there will be no personal income tax cut and no business tax cut.
We see the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) arranging a conference of first ministers, and one wonders what they are going to talk about. One of the commentators today said there

cannot be too much to that conference because the press and the media will be allowed to see what is going on, which in itself is a change of base. The other comment was that the letter of invitation which went out to the first ministers was 11 pages long. The Prime Minister had not much to say in those 11 pages. We are drifting and floating.
The Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Cullen) was in Toronto a few months ago. Speaking to a business group he said that if the business community was not prepared to increase its investment and create more jobs, the government was going to do it. When we look at the mess in the Post Office, I wonder who on the government side will do this.
Look at Air Canada, and at the mess in CNR and DREE. You name it, Mr. Speaker, there is hardly a department in government that has not some real problems. These are the people who plan to bring the Canadian economy back into some semblance of order. I do not think they have the horse sense on the other side to do it. These are the people in the main who got us into this mess and 1 cannot see them getting us out. The only way in which I can show my indignation over the lack of action is to say that when the vote comes, I do not intend to support the bill.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, thank God we are on third reading of the bill so that we do not have to consider it clause by clause; but I think it is important that the appropriate place to have considered the bill clause by clause was during the debate in committee.
The matters which I wish to speak about have been, to some extent, untouched as a result of the closure motion which was imposed on the debate. It is really a sad comment upon the way we do business in this place that somehow we cannot find a rational way of examining something which is as important as a tax bill. Perhaps we could spend less time on some legislation, but surely a tax bill deserves an intensive and meaningful examination by experts in the House, members of parliament who specialize in this matter, with a committee of people considering it over an extensive period of time. We should all have a look at the procedures in this place so that we do not keep running into the problem of our most important piece of legislation going through by default. That is exactly what will happen this week with regard to the bill, 1 am sure.
The purpose behind any income tax legislation from time immemorial has been the redistribution of income. Along with that question of redistributing income, the spin-off from that has been that we use it as a lever in the economy to increase employment or to cure whatever ills there may be from time to time. There is no question that today unemployment is the key problem right across the country. When you examine the fiscal approach to income tax which this government has displayed you find that this legislation will have a negative effect on employment creation.
1 want to deal with that a little more extensively, but before doing so I would like to take a look at what we have been doing over the last 10 or 15 years with regard to our fiscal approach to income tax. Since the Second World War most

December 12, 1977
Income Tax
modern western industrial governments have been engaged in creating what I think is probably improperly called the welfare state. We have attempted, through income tax and through various welfare schemes, to redistribute income. It has been the conventional wisdom amongst all political parties that in fact it is desirable that we provide for those who live in our society more equality of income; in short, that we provide more at the bottom and, if possible and necessary, reduce the incomes of those at the top.
In fact, in 1951 when professor Gillespie of Carleton University did an extensive study of this, the poorest fifth of our population accounted for 4.4 per cent of the money income in Canada. In that same year the richest fifth were taking 42.8 per cent of the money income in Canada. Twenty-five years later, after the alleged progressive income tax bill, after significant changes in the old age pension, significant changes in family allowance and significant changes in unemployment insurance, in 1975 the poorest fifth of our population has had their share of the money income reduced to 3.9 per cent and the richest fifth of the population has continued to take 42.4 per cent of the money income. After all these years we have not changed the relationship between the poorest and the richest in Canada.
We have, of course, increased the pay packet. How much real increase there has been is debatable, but the increase in the pay packet has not been the problem. The problem in Canada continues to be the disparity in incomes between regions and between people, and this particular bill not only does not redress this problem, as I will argue, but it makes the problem considerably worse because of the tax provisions, particularly under RRSPs and child care deductions. It continues to redistribute income in reverse by giving those with higher incomes the largest benefits.
We have not had very much in original throught from the government in terms of income tax changes. In the United States we have had the new administration, the Carter administration, starting to examine some of the realities of income tax. One of these realities is something referred to as the three-martini lunch.

speechtext:
The three-beer lunch is equally deductible if you are lucky enough to be a businessman. If we look at the present deduction provisions in Canada, the amount of revenue that is lost as a result of those unreal deductions-deductions that are only marginally connected to the question of whether they were incurred in the course of doing business-we could find that the amount of tax we would have to impose on the average or lower level taxpayer could be substantially reduced.
I agree with those who say we have to plug the loopholes that lead to waste in public expenditures, but let us remember there is also waste in the private sector.
As I travel across Canada at public expense and see my friends who travel from Vancouver to Toronto and back to
[Mr. Leggatt.)
attend important meetings, I am not always convinced that such meetings are necessary. If they were not tax deductible there would not be so many. As a result, companies would have more profit, or more money to invest in employment, or, as the hon. member for Halton-Wentworth (Mr. Kempling) suggested, in research and development.
We have to look at the three-martini lunch in this country too. We have to look at a tax structure which shows the operator of a Shell gas station paying a lot of tax whilst the Shell company pays almost none. The operator wonders about the tax system that allows major multinational oil companies to escape with massive deferred taxes whilst he pays through the nose. Those are some of the changes that have not been examined, Mr. Speaker.
If we went back to the Carter Commission principle and decided to tax money as it flows, from whatever source, we could begin to have a genuinely progressive tax system. We have built in so many exemptions, so many anomalies, so many devices that were apparently justified at the time they were argued for, we have given in to so many pressure groups, that only accountants can understand the statute and sometimes not even they.
We have a tax system which lacks principle and lacks a theme. The real tragedy of the rejection of the Carter report is that we could have begun to provide some principle to back up the income tax system. Carter said we should not make distinctions between types and sources of income. When we rejected that principle I believe we also rejected our capacity to redistribute income in Canada. As long as we continue to permit anomalies and loopholes, they continue to exist in a graduated tax scheme, to the advantage of those at the upper end of the tax scale.
If in the last 20 years we compare the percentage of income tax paid by the corporate sector and the personal sector, the corporate sector continues to pay less and less of the total. I offer the following examples. In 1961, 30.5 per cent of the total revenues of the federal government came from personal income tax and 22.7 per cent from corporate income tax. In 1976 the personal sector was paying 43.5 per cent and the corporate sector share dropped to 15.7 per cent. That argues for a further examination of the way we tax.
Since I am arguing in favour of the Carter position, I should point out it was also his position that we should integrate entirely personal and corporate tax. Instead of having a 20 per cent dividend credit, Carter argued that the entire scheme could be integrated. I could accept that as rationalizing the tax system as long as those rates were genuinely progressive.
What we have had is a tax system which has not redistributed income because in the corporate area the capacity for deductions is almost endless. People in business have a tremendous scope and range in their deductions. If we eliminated corporate taxes, if we integrated it entirely, as long as it was progressive and redistributed income in Canada-which it does not-then I would say Carter was on the right track.
December 12, 1977

We talk about the person who runs a gas station, works long hours and pays what he believes to be an unfair tax and what I believe to be an unfair tax. The total amount of deferred tax from the oil sector alone-and I am only talking about major companies-is SI,036 million. That kind of money would go a long way toward a guaranteed annual income. If we do not think about moving toward a guaranteed annual income or a refund of tax credit, then nothing is going to be done about unemployment. The idea that unemployment is something out there is a vacuum does not work. Unemployment is created when there is a lack of purchasing power over a large section of the community. It grows like a snowball, and each time someone is laid off, the consuming public is reduced by one.
When the president of Ford Motors asked Walter Reuther what he was going to do when the plant was automated, he replied that he did not see that as the problem. He said, "Who are you going to sell cars to when nobody is working in the plant?" We have to adjust the income tax system to provide purchasing power for people at the low end of the income scale. When you help people of low income you are doing more to spur the economy than at any other level. Someone earning $7,000 or less will spend tax credits if they are made refundable. The money will go back into the economy for food and essentials and thus is a spur to the economy. This income tax bill fails to look seriously not merely at the distribution of wealth but at the whole question of creating employment.
In 1974-and I am sure the latest figures are worse-there were 252 people in Canada with incomes of over $50,000, who paid no tax whatsoever. Under the provisions of the Income Tax Act this was perfectly legitimate. But I would like to examine the equity of each and every one. I think that those who have consistently paid their tax, have not looked for loopholes and have not gone for setting off holding companies etc., to pay their tax, have a right to be represented in this place when 252 people pay no income tax whatsoever.
Of people who file income tax returns, the lowest 70 per cent receive 40 per cent of the tax subsidy benefit. The top 11 per cent get what is an incredible 33 per cent. That has been the effect of what has been alleged to be a progressive income tax system. The National Council of Welfare estimates the federal government lost $6.4 billion in revenue as a result of the exemptions and loop holes, and all of the funny little things that had been built into this system as a result of lobbyists from one part of the community or the other. If you had that $6.4 billion you would not have to worry. You would have a guaranteed annual income scheme. You would not need to worry about it in the future. That represents something like 20 per cent of the federal budget. There is not much question that we have not been redistributing income in Canada.
When the RRSP system came in, people ran around and said, "Good, we have this nice tax shelter for the average guy instead of somebody who is really well off'. The facts are the reverse. People of average income get almost no benefit whatsoever from the RRSP.

speechtext:
About $12,000. This provision of the income tax cost Canadians in revenue $513 million. That is another provision which not only does not redistribute income, it redistributes it in reverse. For example, if you were earning less than $5,000, your tax saving with an RRSP would be $1.02. If you are earning over $20,000, your tax saving is $551.88. So on a dollar basis the RRSP has done a wonderful job of making the rich richer and the poor poorer.
1 agree it is desirable to try to keep Canadian capital at home to encourage Canadian savings. But this is the wrong way to go about it. It does not make any kind of contribution. At the moment Canadians are saving as if it were going out of style. The problem is not Canadians saving; the problem is Canadians are not spending. To move the economy forward, Canadians must spend. Ask any bank manager or credit union manager and they will tell you savings were never better. But they are also finding that foreclosures were never more frequent than they are right now. Funds that people are now starting to squirrel away must be shaken loose in terms of consumption, not in terms of capital investment, because as so many speakers have indicated before in this House we have lots of unused capacity. There is not much point in increasing our capacity. What we need to do is increase our purchasing power.
The next area of income redistribution in reverse is the provision for child care deductions. Those deductions have been doubled under the bill. The child maximum is now $1,000, rather than $500, and the per family maximum goes up from $2,000 to $4,000. If you are at a $10,000 income level, a $1,000 deduction is worth a tax saving of $210. If you are in a $50,000 income category it is worth $430. Exactly the same process. Those with the highest incomes receive the most benefit from this particular tax legislation and those with the lowest incomes receive the least benefit. I see the Parliamentary Secretary shaking his head. In fact, that is unassailable logic. There is really no argument that can be presented with regard to that particular provision.
What can we do? What are the positive things that we can do in terms of making this bill a progressive bill?

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext: Scrap it.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
First of all, it has been said many times that we have $1.2 billion in tax concessions. If we took that $1.2 billion and put it in at the lower level as a tax credit, we could create 100,000 to 150,000 jobs in Canada as a result of increased demand. Again, that should go in the form of tax credits. In other words, let the person who does not have sufficient income to pay tax file a return and receive a refund cheque. That cheque will be spent as soon as it is received, and it will be spent on the products of manufacturers who are crying for purchasers. They are not crying for any more tax hand-outs. They have all the tax hand-outs they need, and they have not done anything. They have not created any employment. But it will create employment if we provide people with

December 12, 1977
Income Tax
purchasing power at the low end who will spend it on essentials-food, clothing and furniture.
The $400 million capital works program was supposed to create 60,000 jobs. That is the same program that was in place in 1971, and is as cautious and as conservative as anyone can get. We have moved so far right in this country that even that one does not appeal and it makes the Conservatives blush when it is rejected by a Liberal government.
We have $500 million allocated to housing and urban transit. That is hardly revolutionary. Certainly the urban transit section was promised in the last election and 1 am sure we will have it promised again in the next election. There is one thing the government does not like, and that is to waste a promise by keeping it; they like to make the same one over again.
Last but not least, there is $50 million assistance to the small businessmen. Let me tell the government what they are doing to the small businessman in my community. If I want to buy textiles or shoes made in central Canada, I am happy as a Canadian to pay a tariff to keep workers working in Ontario and Quebec, and to some extent in the Maritimes. But what I object to is when the government not only puts a tariff on such goods, but puts a quota on them as well. This means you cannot bring goods into the country, no matter what the price is. In British Columbia the people of the lower mainland say: "Well, if that is what you are going to do I will just go to Bellingham and buy it, because it is available there." Who suffers? The small businessman in my community who cannot bring those products into his store but whose competitors do across the border.
We complain about Canadians being competitive. Here we are with a provision which denies the merchants of the lower mainland an opportunity to compete with the people across the border-at any price. Many people purchasing goods in British Columbia would be happy to pay more if they could obtain the product, but they cannot. I can recite a whole range of products that are not available because of this dumb quota system that has been imposed. It has driven the small businessman absolutely round the bend in British Columbia. What happens when we in British Columbia stand and say we will pay the tariff, but at least let us bring the goods in? When I asked the Prime Minister the other day about where we were going to build our ships in our twenty-ship replacement program, why, we are going to buy six of them abroad! We are not going to use the shipyards in British Columbia or Nova Scotia. We are going to go abroad for that. British Columbians are tired of that kind of attitude. We are willing to pay the price of being Canadian, but do we have to pay double? That is what we are going to do. Canadian workers and Canadian shipyards are not being used sufficiently to build those ships. We will not merely be paying more for products that are being protected, but we do not even allow our merchants a decent chance to compete with their competitors across the border. That is an example of the industrial strategy that this government exercises.
The last thing I want to deal with is an idea that is long overdue. That is the question of a refundable tax credit system. Call it a guaranteed annual income. Call it anything you want. Almost every province in Canada has gone on record as favouring a refundable tax system. I can go through the provinces, starting with British Columbia which did a study in August 1977. I quote from page 2 of the August 1977 study of that cautious and conservative government:
The province of British Columbia recommends, therefore, that the premiers appoint a committee representing all provinces to inquire into the basis upon which a refundable tax credit scheme could be developed and implemented for all Canadians.
The point is the same. A tax credit or tax refundable system puts money in the hands of those who will spend it, and will start getting this economy back on its feet. As long as we have this dog in the manger attitude, this completely cautious, unchanged attitude in terms of the way this government treats income tax, we cannot spur the economy. Another example is the cautious Ontario Conservative government, and I quote:
-the recently announced federal tax credit of $50 per child is a further improvement to the current structure-because the value of this reduction is generally independent of income. However, the credit is not refundable, and so its advantage to low-income persons is limited.
That statement is found in the Ontario tax study No. 14, Ministry of Treasury, Economics and Intergovernmental Affairs. Other governments have done some thinking about this, but not this one. There is no original thinking going on.
I will give one minister some credit for having done a bit of thinking about it. Unfortunately, we can never tell if she is being quoted accurately. The Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) said some very interesting things about the idea of a guaranteed annual income or refundable tax credit. I hope she will not be up in her place tomorrow denying that she said this, but I quote from the November 8 issue of the Globe and Mail:
This is sometimes called a negative income tax.
She said three groups-low-income workers, one-parent families and unemployed workers between 50 and 65-would be the initial targets of a program which ultimately could reform the entire welfare system-
Tax credits, such as those for political contributions, are set at fixed levels and give rich and poor the same benefit at tax return time. Rich and poor, for instance, deduct the same amount on their tax forms for children-
"Tax exemptions favour the rich but tax credits favour the poor," she said. "The tax system shouldn't be loaded in favour of any group."
I certainly welcome that statement by the Minister of National Health and Welfare. I hope it represents government policy, but 1 wait in some agony when 1 look at this tax legislation, which does not have an iota of this principle behind it. In fact, it has gone in the reverse direction. I wish the minister had fought a little harder in cabinet to get these very fine principles that she enunciated. I see the former minister of national health and welfare is agreeing to this. In any event, somebody should have been fighting in cabinet to get these refundable tax credits into the piece of nothing tax legislation we are now looking at.
[Mr. Leggatt.l
December 12, 1977

1 left out reference to two very important governments. One was the government of the province of British Columbia which pioneered this question of providing a "mincome" for people, seeing that poor people are well looked after. The NDP government of Manitoba of all governments has probably done the most. They actually instituted and have in place a negative income tax scheme.
I want to give a few examples of that previous government's program; I hope their successors will continue it. In that province, if your income is at the $3,000 level, you can receive a tax refund from the provincial government of $529. That is the maximum they allow. Imagine the effect that could have on the total economy, having a cheque in hand and being able to spend the money on products of manufacturers who are sitting idle looking for purchasers and consumers. There is no indication, other than the obiter dicta of the Minister of National Health and Welfare, that anyone has any real appreciation of this problem.
Let me put it another way. We spend a lot of time talking about DREE grants and regional disparities. The real regional disparities are not DREE grants. They result from the income tax system. The poorest people get the worst break on income tax. Newfoundland and the maritimes, which have the lower average income people, have been shafted by this Income Tax Act. They have not been shafted by DREE because those provinces have not enough attention in terms of capital direction. But their people remain at the low levels of income and are not given the income tax breaks that the rich are given. That is where you find the real disparities of income tax. I wish the rich people of Newfoundland and Nova Scotia would pay some attention to that particular problem. On an average basis, they have suffered the most in terms of this particular principle.
In order to redistribute income, we have to abandon the principle of universality. It is a principle that has been cherished in my party for a very long time. I can understand the rationale behind it. In fact, the provincial governments for some time now have accepted and realized you cannot redistribute income on the universality principle.
If we decided to raise the old age pension to $250 using the principle of universality, that would result in only an additional $7 a month to an income tested recipient. However, it would result in an increase of $107 to someone who is not income tested; in other words, someone who already has a substantial income. It is time we in this House, and I might say we in this party, abandoned that particular principle. In fact, it militates against the redistribution of income to those at lower income levels.
I feel exactly the same way about the debate that raged before I came to this House on the FISP program, or the question of family allowances. Family allowances have to be based on an income tested basis in order to be just. You can no longer use the argument that it is a tax back. I will not accept that argument until we get to a 100 per cent level of tax, and it is probably not desirable that we ever do.
Income Tax
We have to go to the income tested principle behind the payment of a guaranteed annual income and the payment of family allowances-the whole umbrella of welfare services. There was a time when it was very degrading to have a means test. That has now gone. We are now able simply to look at tax returns to determine income levels. Since that onerous provision has been taken away, we in this House must now abandon the principle of universality and get down to the job of redistributing income to the poor. We cannot do that when we make every program universally acceptable. It is just not cost effective and it is not wise because we do not tax all of that money back.
