speechtext: Will the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Leggatt) tell me whether the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) agrees with his philosophy on this matter?

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext: He knows I don't.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
The answer is no. I think this Chamber would be a very odd place if we all agreed with each other on everything. I know one thing, though. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) and I are going in the same direction and we are members of the only party that is; everyone else has abondoned the concept.
Since reference has been made to my hon. friend 1 might say that the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre has made a larger contribution to the redistribution of wealth in Canada than any other person I know; so when we do have a difference of opinion about the best approach to take-and we do disagree publicly in this party from time to time; we disagree in this chamber-it does not detract one whit from my hon. friend's contribution.
I end with a plea to the government. I have no hope we can block this bill, but surely in the next piece of legislation of this type we could begin to go about the serious business of providing a guaranteed annual income or a refundable tax credit for those who fall below the income tax line. Until we do this we shall not be able to accomplish anything meaningful with respect to the redistribution of income in Canada.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before I make my main speech I would like to mention something I had not thought of till now. There is in my town an experiment started by the NDP government, funded primarily by the federal government, on the effect of a guaranteed income in a community of approximately 10,000 people both rural and urban. While the details of minimum income are closely guarded there are certain obvious things one can see, and from what I understand after discussing the matter with the people involved there is evidence that most interesting and untoward changes have occurred. For example, people arrange their incomes so as to take advantage of the income guaranteed, by the state. If everyone was on a salary and if every dollar that came in by whatever means could be recorded, administration

December 12, 1977
Income Tax
might be easier, but in many cases it is extremely difficult to determine the actual income of a particular person or family.
I think we should wait for the results. It appears they will not be assessed for some time but I understand from those who are knowledgeable on the subject that the figures really do not prove anything. They do not prove whether a guaranteed income would work or not, though there are instances where industry was perhaps retarded among individuals who were content to accept what the pay was and let it go at that. I might just add that if anyone wants to think a guaranteed annual income is an easy thing to administer, that it is a cure-all and a panacea, he is mistaken.
In this third reading debate I would like to comment on one or two things. The budgetary changes are not particularly sweeping. Despite a little tinkering here and there they have not changed the situation a great deal. It is unfortunate that closure was invoked in the Committee of the whole stage because certain clauses should have been tested and discussed more carefully.
I would like to dwell on the roll-over provisions, especially with that portion which has to do with capital gains. The mere fact that the government has had to introduce modifications to this tax shows that it is virtually impossible to administer with any degree of fairness without causing serious loss of business, which is the lifeblood of our communities.
During the long debate on the capital gains tax and in dicussion of the white paper on taxation and the subsequent legislation arising out of it, the issue of capital gains arose time and again and we heard a great deal of evidence about the difficulty of assessing capital gains and their subsequent taxation. We heard how in the United Kingdom such files were laid aside because only very senior tax people could work on them. This meant that many years elapsed before complex situations were clarified with resultant uncertainty and dislocation in business. If capital gains tax were introduced on the basis that it was a fair way to tax-and on the surface there is much to suggest this-time has proved that increase of property values which occurs over a lifetime of business is largely a reflection of the inflationary situation of our day. Slavish adherence to the capital gains tax is really a salute to the philosophy of Carter that a buck is a buck and should always be taxed by any manner or means.
In the United States, where the experience was similar to that of the United Kingdom, Congress at the turn of the century passed laws imposing capital gains tax and then spent a great deal of time passing further laws providing loopholes in order to obviate undesirable effects on the economy.
Capital gains tax is difficult to administer. It is regressive and inimical to family business continuity, let alone expansion. No one quarrels very much with the theory that those who buy and sell farms, properties, et cetera, should pay a tax if they do so regularly and are making a living out of it. But the capital gains tax is detrimental in that it hits hardest at those who buy for production, those who spend a lifetime building up a business or establishment only to find that much of their gain is lost through the capital gains tax. If there were no inflation

or if the capital gains tax took into account the inflation rate, there could be some redress. But the situation with respect to capital gains shows there should be a wholesale re-evaluation of the value of this tax. We should examine whether or not it should be done away with altogether or whether it should be drastically changed.
When the capital gains tax was introduced its main intention was not to unduly tax businesses and proprietorships that were of long standing, but to catch the individual who was using the no-capital-gains-tax-situation to buy and sell on short intervals, thus circumventing the normal income tax levies. But the Department of National Revenue had moved to close many of these loopholes before the capital gains tax was even instituted, so it is possible that this tax is now doing considerably more damage than its value. It is felt most severely not by the extremely wealthy or by the large corporations but rather by individuals whose assets are tied up in a small business. If there is to be a capital gains tax it would seem to be more logical that we introduce it on a diminishing basis, as is common in some western countries. If it is meant to catch the individual who buys and sells for profit rather than for the sake of acquiring a productive instrument, surely a diminishing rate of tax should be paid on the capital gains portion. It seems logical to me that if a person holds a piece of productive property for ten years he should pay no capital gains tax.
The present legislation broadens the capital gains principle but in theory at least it recognizes that the tax has serious disadvantages and that it impedes the roll-over of farms and small businesses. Its effect is merely to postpone the tax bill and sooner or later a business will be largely wiped out by the tax liability it will incur. Nevertheless, a quarter of a loaf is better than nothing.
I would like to reiterate the comment I made during committee of the whole, that the important thing will be what is the interpretation of the changes which the government has proposed. As regards farming, it seems that it is going to be very narrowly interpreted and perhaps confined only to land. There should be some way in which regulations should be at least outlined when legislation is introduced.
Furthermore, the intentions of the government can be seriously reduced by the actions of tax officials. My experience has been that our tax system is not particularly sympathetic to individuals who are in business on their own. There is a general feeling amongst many, perhaps because most people are wage earners, that individual businessmen and farmers make too much money and somehow are able to not pay their fair share of tax. There seems to be some change in the public perception of business, as many now realize that a high standard of living necessitates a vigorous and active business climate.
I should like to refer to what is being said about our general economic situation. The present issue of "Canada's Energy
December 12, 1977

Resources", issued by the Canada-Japan Trade Council, at page 8 reads as follows:
Canada is a nation heavily dependent on foreign trade. We cannot achieve prosperity by continuing to borrow many billions yearly, much from outside Canada, to pay for governmental deficits and provide social services or offset deficits in balance-of-payments. That's the road, if followed too long, to national bankruptcy. It is employment of people in producing goods and services, generating what can be sold at a profit in Canada or abroad, that is needed to bring better balance to both the internal and the external accounts of the nation. Our "Energy Potential" is one of Canada's greatest means of achieving these desirable and needed ends.
There is no point discussing the merits of a guaranteed annual income if we do not have the goods and services necessary to bring that into effect.
A veteran political columnist, Bruce Hutchinson, in the Ottawa Journal of December 1 published a column called "Two Nations Deep in Economic Trouble". He pointed out economic policies in Washington and Ottawa have followed a course of zig-zags and U-turns, with an unknown destination. It seems that experts in the economy certainly agree that the North American economy is not likely to become much richer in the immediate future, and if there is not wise management, can be a lot poorer.
In the United States the Carter administration has deserted its original design of high prosperity and low inflation and has gone into pump priming, reminiscent of the new deal decade with its tax cuts and huge budgetary deficits. Nor is there much disagreement in Congress about these tax reductions except on details. The U.S. government will run a deficit estimated at $58 billion and next year this will be much larger. Even so, considering the size of our economy, our national deficit of $9 billion plus is still relatively one-third higher than that of the United States. In fact, we are considerably worse off than the United States, and anyone can ask whether larger spending and deficits will assure satisfactory economic growth and full employment. Furthermore, the provincial budgets are showing real deficits.
Turning to the international side, the United States will run a foreign trade deficit of $20 billion to $30 billion, but as Canada's net deficit will be $5 billion, in U.S. terms this would mean $60 billion. Canada's growth rate will be half or less than the U.S. rate, while its inflation rate will be 2 percentage points higher. By most standards, in a country well endowed with natural resources we have brought ourselves to a sorry spot in our economy.
If it were just the economy alone that was in trouble, that would be one thing. We are in trouble in a political way- whether or not Quebec remains within confederation. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) has listed the problems that are piling up: loss of population, businesses moving out of the province, and a faster rate of unemployment than in the rest of Canada. Slowly but surely Quebec is divorcing itself from the rest of the country, as is evidenced by the Globe and Mail article entitled: "The Black View of Canada from Abroad".
The latest indication of this is in the francophonization of companies. A corporate official of a national company head-
Income Tax
quartered in Quebec had this to say: "It is becoming more and more apparent to us that employees in English Canada are becoming less and less enthusiastic about working for a Quebec based corporation." Some Quebec executives are complaining that there is an unfortunate nationalization taking over in English Canada. Buyers will purchase products from all over the world, but some say: "We wish you weren't located in Quebec." It is the hardening in the rest of the country against the unreasonable situations that are present in that province, which is quite understandable. Telephone calls by private individuals in the rest of Canada to business in Quebec invariably turn up only francophone speaking individuals, and the smaller the individual businessman, the worse the situation is. Naturally distributors and merchants in other parts of Canada attempt to procure new sources when their supplies are diminished. Some might say this is unfair but it is quite a natural reaction. Not only is this political situation hurting Quebec, but it is also hurting the rest of Canada. It is hurting our image abroad.
When Mr. Davis of Ontario went to Japan, as well as the usual complaint that Canadians produce poorly, he had to refute the possibility of Quebec separation, a refutation that one can question is seriously valid. Fortune magazine has told its business readers that the threat of separation has produced a lack of capital, securities and potential investment in Quebec. There is a very black view taken by a correspondent writing in Finance-Seer, a journal directed to businessmen in the United States. He points out that the PQ leaders are greatly underestimated, and because they have downgraded their plans for a new currency, a new Quebec central bank and a Quebec army, it does not mean they have given them up. He points out that foreign bankers and investors might wake up to the fact that their loans are being paid for in worthless Quebec dollars.
Many of the problems of the Canadian economy may be traced to excessive government spending, with a whole host of programs in the social welfare field. As Canadians found that the necessity to pay and save money for individual care diminished as in the health field, their tax dollars were funnelled to Ottawa and redistributed to the provinces.
This has created great strains on confederation, so much so that it is now in danger of breaking up. Canadians were a lot happier when the people of each region had to look after their own health, welfare and education. This may have brought with it a certain amount of inequity, but this was preferable to the present situation.
Some of these untoward effects in our economy were initiated long ago, but certainly the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and a past minister of finance, who now lives in Toronto, Mr. Turner, must bear a great deal of the blame for the bad news. That national unemployment rate is 8.4 per cent. Inflation is accelerating. The real labour income of the worker is diminishing, estimated by some to be 4.3 per cent last year. There is a record high current account deficit, with record borrowing abroad. Our budget deficit is some $9 billion and will be higher next year. Our resource industries are falling

December 12, 1977
Income Tax
behind. They have been one feature of the economy which has presented us with stability, stemming from the decision of the budget of 1973, when Mr. Turner said, in speaking of overshooting the target, the following:
We recognize that we are running a risk, and that the risk is on the side of overshooting. That is a risk worth taking at this time in the interest of dealing more effectively with unemployment.
It is clear that the Prime Minister and Mr. Turner have lost the gamble. The long years of increased social benefits culminated in the rich and expensive unemployment insurance scheme. With low interest rates and a booming economy, there was too much money in circulation and inflation became double digited.
The decision to keep the domestic oil price significantly below the U.S. level has had its effect, and we have not adapted to this. With our domestic supplies of oil diminishing, we have still to take this step. There does not seem to be any doubt that the increase in the price of oil which will eventually have to come about, will come about when we least wish it. High unemployment was aggravated by the long period of wage and price controls. Had they been short and sharp, the high rise in unemployment would have been stopped, but the uncertainty of many companies in dealing with the Anti-Inflation Board has caused the economy to slip into stagnation. How things have changed since the former minister of finance, Mr. Turner, said in his May, 1974 budget:
We Canadians today have reached at threshold of great challenge and great opportunity.
We have a great opportunity to demonstrate our ability to deal with the deflated economy, with unemployment and with our political realities in regard to the province of Quebec. Nearly all top flight financial people feel that the most important mistake was the overexpansion of our money supply in the 1972-1974 period. It was aided by the high profits accruing to resource and corporate producers, with higher government taxes and higher wages which were not reduced once the commodity boom was over.
Our economy has been badly managed in these few years and we are seeing the result of it still. Even the Prime Minister has said there is no immediate turn around in sight. This budget does little to give confidence to Canadians that we are doing anything more than what the hon. member for Halton-Wentworth (Mr. Kempling) called drifting.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to say a few words on third reading of Bill C-ll. 1 have been in my seat most of the time listening to various speakers. I listened with considerable interest and participated myself during committee of the whole stage. This bill, as we know, suffered the guillotine of closure last Friday. As I mentioned at that time, the opposition and parliament as a whole should not debate this bill ad infinitum without any foreseeable end to the debate, but I believe there were about 16 clauses which we had considered in detail and the 16th clause was passed around 3.30 p.m. Friday afternoon. But the

100 clauses that were left went through by 4.15 p.m. or 4.30 p.m. with great speed and with no debate. As was pointed out by some hon. members during the debate today, a good many of these 100 clauses merited some thought and discussion. I wanted to bring that to the attention of the House.
I am particularly interested in some of the clauses. I am not a lawyer and I am not too familiar with some of these tax credits, but there were certain items which, speaking as a layman and speaking on behalf of a great many taxpayers in the low tax bracket or even on behalf of those who do not pay taxes, merit some comments from me.
First and foremost, the ordinary working man who, prior to this legislation, received an allowance of $150 for business expenditures has felt that this was not sufficient, and the government in its generosity has increased it to $250, which is certainly not very much. I know hon. members opposite will agree that $250 is not a great deal of money in this inflationary period because there are many workers who must drive some distance to their place of work and who must have meals away from home during the pursuit of their jobs. As I said, this includes construction workers. I mentioned to you in particular, Mr. Speaker, that this applies also to railroaders with whose problems you are certainly familiar. I assume you were more familiar with them a few years ago than you are at present, but I am quite sure you have lent a sympathetic ear to that request.
An amendment was brought in requesting that the government reconsider the amount and bring it up to $400. This amendment was defeated and I am sorry that was the case. A great many of these workers have legitimate costs which are pretty high and which they can document. It seems rather unfair that a businessman can deduct his expenses but a good many other workers who have as just a cause cannot. I might say, having been a rural insurance agent for a great number of years and a real estate broker later, that I am well aware that it cost me a lot of money to do business, but I was able to deduct legitimate business expenses. The tax man probably did not look at them all as legitimate and threw out a good many of them, but I guess that is the name of the game.
One other item which was of particular interest to me was the amendments dealing with life insurance. The clauses were amended and the bill, so far as life insurance is concerned, was certainly considerably improved. Originally, when life insurance proceeds were to be paid at death, death tax would be imposed which was, as we said, almost robbing the grave and stealing from widows and orphans. I think that struck home and the government amended the clause.
Another legitimate amendment concerned deduction of interest on a legitimate insurance loan for business purposes, and I recall government members' reaction at the time I proposed this. I can still hear the former minister of finance as much as telling me I was crazy to even consider that. Thank the Lord the majority of the House is crazy along with me, because the government has accepted my proposal to deduct the interest on insurance loans as a legitimate business expense.
December 12, 1977

There is only one kicker left and I wish to bring it to the attention of the House, namely, that if a loan is made on a life insurance policy and happens to be more than the premium, it is considered as income for the year. As I pointed out to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) and his parliamentary secretary, I doubt there would be more than one in a thousand loans that would qualify under that provision, because in a great number of loans made on life insurance policies the interest which would be eligible as a deductible expense would not be as much as the loan. I felt that because of the bookwork and all the problems the department-I assume it would be the Department of National Revenue-would have in trying to collect those isolated taxes, it would be hardly worth the candle. I wanted to bring that to the attention of the government and in particular the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lumley), who I am pleased to see present here.
The so-called budget-"so-called" because at the time it was supposed to be just a ways and means motion-is supposed to do a good deal of things to generate activity in the economy and provide jobs, but when we ask how many jobs will be generated as a result, many of us are pessimistic, to say the least.
We all know that the unemployment rate is at a high 8.4 per cent. 1 believe that is the highest since 1940, and it is a cause of serious concern to all of us. Programs are in place to provide jobs. The Canada Works Program is of a temporary nature. It is certainly welcome-there is no question about that-but in my riding there is high seasonal unemployment. In Parry Sound-Muskoka I believe we were allotted $1.1 million, which was considerably more than many other ridings, but considerably less than some others. That amount will provide only 311 jobs, and only for a fixed period of time. Something has to be done to put more money into the economy.
It has been suggested-and I agree-that the sales tax is a regressive tax. It hits everybody. It hits those people who do not make enough money even to pay income tax. If the sales tax was reduced, a great deal more money would be put into the economy. People would benefit because they could purchase more goods and services. That would certainly improve the economy.
I come back to what I suppose is a pet theme of mine, that is, the 10-cent federal sales tax on gasoline. To me that is a very bad tax. I believe it was imposed on July 1, 1975. It was imposed to balance our oil accounts, I suppose. Then we were told it was to help conserve gasoline. However, the amount of gasoline which has been saved or which has not been used because of that 10-cent tax is infinitesimal. I said earlier that we might have saved 100 gallons, but it has probably not even been that amount. People are still driving their cars. They still need their cars. Many people use their cars for business purposes. For them, using their cars is a necessity. Working people can deduct the cost of their gasoline, trucks and cars as
Income Tax
legitimate business expenses, and I agree with that. However, the majority of people are not pleasure drivers; they are not Sunday drivers; they have to use their vehicles, whether they be half-ton trucks or cars, to drive up to 100 miles a day and return. Sometimes they drive even further than that. In order to keep their jobs they have to pay those expenses, and many people feel like quitting because it costs so much to get to and from their jobs. The alternative is welfare or drawing unemployment insurance for the first while.
Most people are proud and want jobs, and if the government will not cancel this 10-cent gasoline tax, the tax should be reduced by seven cents to three cents. A recommendation of that kind was made by the tourist industry. The amount collected by the government since July 1, 1975 with this 10-cent surtax is absolutely astronomical. I would be very interested in knowing what that amount is.
We must cut down on the cost of government. Government expenditures are very high and are very difficult to restrain. We are living in a time of restraint. Various ministers including the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) have stated that because of this restraint the public service has been or will be reduced. Fast week the latest figures showed an increase in the public service of, I believe, about 15,000 persons. I believe the public service now numbers 480,000. At this rate the number will be half a million before too long. The government should be looking into this very seriously.
We have made certain concrete and positive suggestions with regard to this bill. The $100 tax allowance for taxpayers is supposed to take place in early 1978. That amount is not very high, and I do not think it will generate very much economic activity. We hoped that allowance would be put in place in 1977 as well as in 1978 and successive years.
As a member of the housing committee I have spoken with some feeling and force on the insulation program. The grant is to be $350 for eight of the provinces. The unfortunate thing is that that $350 is considered to be taxable income. I admit that many old age pensioners, widows and others who are reinsulating will not pay tax on this grant, but many low income families who are receiving just enough to pay income tax are going to have to. They will probably think two or three times before bothering to apply for a re-insulation grant. I was given astronomical figures by the minister, after consultation with his officials, as to what this is going to cost the government. Of course, I took that with a grain of salt. If the government wants the re-insulation program to get off the ground, it should make the grants tax deductible just as it does in Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island. I am aware of high electricity costs in those two provinces, but Parry Sound-Muskoka is not exactly the banana belt of the Dominion of Canada. Yesterday morning it was 34 below zero in Burks Falls where I live, and that is the good Christian temperature, not that crazy Celsius.
Insulation is very necessary for the homes in my area and in other northern areas. Surely to goodness if there are high energy costs in Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island, there are other items of just as much importance which are also

December 12, 1977
Income Tax
expensive in northern Ontario, northern Alberta and other northern parts of the country. People in those areas should also qualify under the re-insulation program so that grants can be deducted from taxable income. There is still some time for the government to recant. I hope it will think this over and admit that its proposal is nonsense. We know the number of people who have applied under this program. I mentioned this during the committee of the whole last week. We also know the number of grants which have been approved and paid. The number is very small compared with what the government expected. Those figures prove that the plan cooked up by the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Gillespie) and the Minister of State for Urban Affairs (Mr. Ouellet) is not successful in creating work. If people would take advantage of this program, that would cut down on energy consumption. 1 hope something will be done in this regard. Clause 116 provided authority for the government to borrow $9 billion. That is another thing that was sneaked in that a lot of us are wondering and worrying about.
The member who spoke previously, the great socialist from New Westminster, made some comments that had merit. He pointed out that 43 per cent of the income tax revenues came from individual taxpayers and a much smaller amount came from corporations. It is because of the items I have mentioned that so much is collected from the ordinary taxpayer. A reduction in the sales tax would benefit everybody and generate more money for the economy. There is also that iniquitous 10-cent tax on gasoline. It is an unfair tax because it penalizes people who cannot claim expenses for driving to and from work as deductible, even in cases where the distance is considerable.
In view of these items, Mr. Speaker, I hope something can be done to amend some of the clauses on third reading. 1 know the bill will probably go through but I am not prepared to vote for it in its present state.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a few short comments to make in this third reading debate which will relate fairly directly to the comments I made on second reading debate on November 17 and in committee of the whole on December 6. On those occasions I dwelt on two major aspects of the impact of this tax bill on Canadian agriculture and I want to dwell on them a little more in some new ways tonight.
The first matter is the serious consequences of the capital gains tax on the roll-over of incorporated family farms and partnerships to the next generation brought about by the ravages of inflation since the advent of the new capital gains approach to the tax system that has been with us for about seven years. This change is distinct from the situation of an individual farmer-one who is not incorporated or in a partnership-who has this privilege of roll-over.
The second matter 1 dwelt on in some detail referred to my representations to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) and other ministers who made up what I think is properly called a

contingency drought committee composed of eight Cabinet ministers. This committee was quite active last spring and summer and I think it is still active in regard to the continuing and worsening drought in southern Alberta and southwestern Saskatchewan. In this area I called for a tax deferral program that would recognize the particular problems brought on by this drought in the cattle industry in southern Alberta and southwestern Saskatchewan. The program would have to last until the drought is over and grass and feed supplies return to more or less normal. This, of course, may take several years.
The proposal to allow a tax deferral program would encourage the necessary cow numbers to be reduced to levels that could be supported on local grass and feed supplies in spite of the considerably larger taxable incomes that would result from this conditional scale down of cattle. I think it was a reasonable suggestion that I made in the course of the earlier debates. It is the prudent course to follow under severe drought conditions instead of buying expensive feed over a long winter. There is now every indication of an extremely cold and long winter. This was the lesson we learned in the drought and depression days of the 1930's, but there were no tax problems then and we did not have to worry about the level of taxable income.
I am pleased to report three weeks after the suggestions were put forward that I have received good support for them from the farm audience over a wide area, including a big part of western Canada, parts of Ontario and even within this House from members of other parties. This gives me some satisfaction. Since preparing those earlier remarks some additional background information has come to my attention with respect to the capital gains roll-over item.
I should like to refer to the 1971 census figures. In that census tabulation there were 21,019 family farm partnerships or 8.1 per cent and another 7,011 family farm corporations or 3.1 per cent. These 29,000, which the census describes as commercial farms, made up 11.2 per cent of all farmers in Canada in 1971 and accounted for at least 20 per cent of total farm production. Some 113,000 commercial farms accounted for about 77.5 per cent of the total production in Canada in 1971. In other words, incorporated family farms and partnerships account for a disproportionately large share of Canadian farm production.
The figures given by the Minister of Finance showing only 2 per cent of farms being incorporated leave the wrong impression. Not only is the percentage too low but the minister did not look at what the 3.1 per cent produced on their farms- over 20 per cent of the total farm production. This is, of course, together with the partnerships. These categories do not enjoy the roll-over privileges for intergenerational transfer that individual farmers now enjoy. I submit that incorporation does not resolve either the liquidity problem or the ability to pay capital gains tax.
Recently there has been some research announced just within the last month. It was done at the University of Guelph,
December 12, 1977

in a study by Gellner and Brinkman. This study found capital gains were an important component of farm returns. Between the years 1971 and 1974 covered by the study, capital gains amounted to 35 per cent of total farm returns. However, the study pointed out that capital gains by contrast on comparable nonfarm business amounted to 25 per cent. The point I am making is, if a distinction can be drawn between unincorporated farm operations and other businesses, and this is so, the same distinction can be drawn between incorporated family farms and farm partnerships on the one hand, and other incorporated businesses on the other hand.
Surely, we now have a travesty of justice as a result of the critical impact of capital gains under extreme inflationary conditions, wherein efficient farmers and ranchers are being taxed out of existence. There can be no real long term gain for government or the nation in taxing our best farmers in a manner to drive them out of their successful business, preventing a logical transfer to the next generation.
I want to associate myself with the remarks made this afternoon by my colleague from Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain (Mr. Hamilton) on roll-over in the corporate structure. His approach to this same subject was most appropriate. 1 also want to associate myself with his appropriate reference to today's lead story in the Toronto Globe and Mail with the headline-it is a catchy headline and an excellent story-"PM Lost Fiscal Gamble-Canada pays with Ailing Economy". I suggest this should be required reading, not only by members of this House but any Canadian who is concerned about our critical economic situation today.
In closing, Mr. Speaker, as I indicated in the committee of the whole in reference to this capital gains roll-over item, there has been no change in the Department of Finance's views for almost three years, yet there has been an incredible increase in the impact of capital gains tax on family and incorporated farms due to our continuing and increasing inflation. Surely a new look now is absolutely essential. I would like to remind the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) of his closing statement to me in the committee when he said:
I should, however, like to find a date which might be suitable, and I will ask my staff to get in touch with the honorable member. If this cannot be arranged, I shall certainly make sure there is a meeting with my officials on this subject.
This, of course, was a reference to my suggestion that Canadian cattle producers would like and deserve the chance to meet with the Minister of Finance and his senior staff on this very important subject. 1 take this opportunity to remind him of that statement and hope that something will come of it. 1 did not mean to imply at that time, nor do 1 now, that it should take place in the heat of this long debate with which we are still involved. I hope, however, that such a meeting, when it comes, is more productive than the last meeting three years ago, at that time with a former minister of finance, Mr. Turner. In spite of two closure motions to get this tax amendment bill to this third reading stage, it is still not too late to call upon the minister to recognize the genuine sincerity of at least some suggestions coming out of this debate. I suggest he implement at least some of them. If not now, then certainly he
Adjournment Debate
should make appropriate plans to incorporate them in the next budget.

I am not going to take much of the House's time, Mr. Speaker, but this debate does provide me with an opportunity to tell the parliamentary secretary, and through him the minister, just what I think of the economic policy of this government. I welcome the few minutes available to me before ten o'clock.
I would like to say to the parliamentary secretary, in the minister's absence, that while there has been much political hay about the economic mess, for which the government is responsible, we must try to make the best of what we have. We have heard about the delays, the stone-walling and the holding back of this important measure, but I wonder if the government knows what it has done to Canadians since last March, even a small group of Canadians, some of whom may be represented in the Liberal caucus. There may even be one or two in ours and elsewhere. Chartered accountants have been sitting behind their desks since March with clients flooding in their doors on the basis of the original budget, which was allowed to die an ignominious death. But no CA has been able to file a return with any degree of certainty whatsoever on the basis of that budget statement.
What has transpired has been this. A client will come in during this last fiscal year and the chartered accountant will say to that client: "I have no idea whether to file under the March budget statement; that was the previous law, I will find out for you". First of all he phones the regional tax office, and they reply: "We do not really know, but you may have an option to file under both; send us an accompanying letter".
Put yourself in the position, not only of the chartered accountant, but of the client to whom he must have given advice since March of this year, almost nine, ten months ago. It is simply inexcusable. If the opposition, according to government spokesmen, lacks integrity for delaying this bill, that lack of integrity is minuscule compared to the lack of fiscal integrity that this government has exhibited since March of this year. Not only has the government been callously indifferent to the economy of the country, but it failed to implement the so-called budget of last March. Then they come roaring in after the throne speech debate and, I suppose, expect passage of the bill within hours. This is simply indefensible.

subtopic: ROYAL CANADIAN MOUNTED POLICE-MINISTER'S USE OF TERMS "NATIONAL SECURITY"
ROYAL CANADIAN MOUNTED POLICE-MINISTER'S USE OF TERMS "NATIONAL SECURITY"
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the minister, on December 6, when asked to define the term "national security" put in the context of the BNA Act or in jurisdictional or legal sense, replied that he took a great deal of guidance from section 16 of the Official Secrets Act. He stated, sir, that the mandate of the security service was derived, almost totally, from that definition-which talks about subversive activities, not national security per se.
What I would like to say to the Solicitor General (Mr. Fox) tonight, in an attempt to be a little provocative, is that he is bandying about the term "national security" as little more than a parliamentary buzz word. He has not, so far, related it in a definitive, constructive way to justify the tactics, legal or political, that he is using vis-a-vis provincial inquiries that are attempts to gather information.
in a recent report dealing with governmental operations with respect to intelligence activities, Mr. Commager noted that in the United States-
-The emergence of intelligence over the past quarter-century as an almost independent branch of the executive, largely immune from either political limitations or legal controls, poses constitutional questions graver than any since the civil war and reconstruction.
Mr. Commager goes on to say that:
The metamorphosis of the two concepts of national security and secrecy are extremely ominous.
He decries the audacity with which the claim of national security is used as a cover for almost anything the executive wishes to do, and notes the casualness with which the term national security has been accepted, a term or phrase unknown to the constitution. He describes it, not as a substantive power, but as a principle in search of a definition, a definition which the Solicitor General, in Canadian parliamentary terms, is unable to provide.
Recently in a Toronto newspaper the Solicitor General was quoted as saying that national security was clearly a federal responsibility under the constitutional provision to provide peace, order, and good government. Of course, he was quoting section 91 of the British North America Act which outlines not only the power of parliament but the restrictions as well. Section 91 reads:
It shall be lawful for the Queen, by and with the consent of the Senate and House of Commons to make laws for the Peace, Order and Good Government of Canada in relation to all matters not coming within the Classes or Subjects by this Act assigned exclusively to the Legislatures of the Provinces.
In my opinion, the term "provide" used by the minister cannot be construed to mean "make" in the act. The latter term means to "legislate"; the former to do a service. To "provide" peace and order can only mean to "administrate and enforce". Thus the government in this case cannot with certainty say that it is responsible constitutionally to provide peace and order in the provinces. That exclusive power is contained in section 92 of the BNA Act, and it relates solely to

the provinces. The 1871 addition to the BNA Act in which it gave temporary authority to parliament to "administer peace and order" in the Territories is support for that opinion.
If an attempt is made to determine just what national security involves, we must refer to law in its present context. There seems to be no statute or definition of national security. The term has been pulled out of thin air. We can therefore only surmise what it may mean.
Section 46 of the Criminal Code deals with treason, et cetera. It also deals with offences such as spying. The Official Secrets Act and War Measures Act are both likely being used to uphold the term "national security". Yet these acts, including the Criminal Code, are, within the meaning of the administration of justice, a provincial responsibility. The Protection of Privacy Act reveals that subversive activity as defined comes within the same meaning.
In an attempt to strengthen or provide legality for federal responsibility, the Solicitor General is in fact saying that the administration of justice in the field of national security is its responsibility. This pseudo axiom is supported by him in the Commons debate of November 15, 1977, page 885 of Hansard:
By convention, the responsibility for national security devolves upon the Prime Minister and is shared with those ministers charged with specific responsibility for the police, external relations and the administration of justice.
It would appear that the present government is on the one hand running the country by convention, but, finding that hat does not fit, is falling back on section 91. The term "administration of justice", as used by the Solicitor General, clearly reveals his government is under the illusion it is responsible for that function. He has yet to face section 92 and the forbidding clauses in section 91.
The divisions of powers between parliament and the provinces are explicitly set out in sections 91 and 92. No matter how the present government attempts to circumvent these sections in justifying its role in national security, it cannot be certain to do so without violating the constitution.
The next step of the government can easily be anticipated. In order that they may constitutionally provide legality for the RCMP Act, they will once again refer to "provide peace and order" under section 91. They might be better advised to look at section 91(27), but that is a variation of a theme. To repeat myself and bring this into context, I am of the firm opinion that the legislating of a police act, excepting in the Territories, can only be done under the authority of section 92 which reads:
In each Province the Legislature may exclusively make Laws in relation to Matters coming within the Classes of Subject next hereafter enumerated, that is to say:
14: The Administration of Justice in the Province . ..
The administration of justice requires laws to be enforced, one of which is a police act. Each province has therefore legislated its own police act. Now if we return to section 91, we find that parliament is expressly forbidden to pass laws coming within the classes of subjects by this act assigned exclusively to the legislatures of the provinces. It, therefore, has absolutely
December 12, 1977

no constitutional authority to pass a police act involving provincial jurisdiction. To me, it is as clear as that.
To continue to fiddle and fuddle around "peace and order", "administration of justice", "conventions" or whatever, is to only further compound those sins of omission and commission which have brought about the present controversy.

subtopic: ROYAL CANADIAN MOUNTED POLICE-MINISTER'S USE OF TERMS "NATIONAL SECURITY"
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the royal commission on security in 1969 made it clear that it was the duty of the state to protect its secrets from espionage, its institutions from subversion and its policies from clandestine influence.
The national security of Canada, understood in its domestic context, includes all of these responsibilities.
The maintenance of such national internal security is the responsibility of the government of Canada. This responsibility is derived not only from statutes and regulations such as those relating to the RCM Police but also from the provisions of the constitutional framework requiring the federal government to maintain peace, order and good government in Canada.
In its operational context, the maintenance of national security is upheld by the RCM Police, specifically the security service. The scope of the mandate of this group is found in law at section 16(3) of the Official Secrets Act. In this section, subversive activity means: (a) espionage or sabotage; (b) foreign intelligence activities directed toward gathering intelligence information relating to Canada; (c) activities directed toward accomplishing governmental change within Canada or elsewhere by force or violence or any criminal means; (d) activities by a foreign power directed toward actual or potential attack or other hostile acts against Canada; or (e) activities of a foreign terrorist group directed toward the commission of terrorist acts in or against Canada.

subtopic: NORTHERN AFFAIRS-PROPOSED CONSTRUCTION OF HIGHWAY BETWEEN FORT McMURRAY AND FORT SMITH-INQUIRY AS TO FEDERAL AID
NORTHERN AFFAIRS-PROPOSED CONSTRUCTION OF HIGHWAY BETWEEN FORT McMURRAY AND FORT SMITH-INQUIRY AS TO FEDERAL AID
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 am taking this opportunity to raise an important matter, one which I have brought to the attention of the House previously on November 9 of this year. It concerns the development of a transportation system which would serve the Northwest Territories, specifically, the construction of two highways directly affecting the economy of the north and more particularly the western part of the Northwest Territories.
The first of these proposed developments is the construction of a gravel highway to link Fort McMurray, Alberta with Fort Smith in the Northwest Territories. I recently met with the deputy premier of Alberta, Dr. Hugh Horner, to discuss this project. Dr. Horner, who is also the Alberta minister of transport, expressed serious and favourable interest in this proposal on behalf of the provincial government. He and 1 both agree that a highway along this route would provide long
Adjournment Debate
term benefits for the province of Alberta and more immediate benefits for the Northwest Territories.
It is clear, however, that a massive project such as this should not be financed solely by a provincial government. I am therefore seeking support from the federal government to enable this development to take place. I am urging that representatives of the government meet with me and with representatives of the Alberta government to discuss the possibility of proceeding with this project. I hope the government of Canada will see to it that a satisfactory financial agreement can be reached in order that work may begin as soon as possible.
The second proposal concerns the construction of the Liard highway to link Fort Nelson, B.C., with Fort Simpson in the Northwest Territories. Construction of such a highway would bring about important benefits for the Northwest Territories, for the Yukon and for British Columbia. In addition, it would open up the agricultural possibilities of the Liard area. I do not think many people are aware of those possibilities but I am firmly of the opinion that there is great agricultural potential in that area.
At present, the British Columbia government has paid for a 20-mile section out of Fort Nelson and a 50-mile stretch which exists in the Northwest Territories from Fort Simpson to Fort William. However, there have not been any serious efforts made to complete the project. I would like to know why the federal government has dragged its feet on this project. I would also like to know when the Treasury Board and the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development are going to make a decision on the construction of the Liard highway. I raised this issue with the President of Treasury Board (Mr. Andras) recently in the House, and was informed that I should have directed my question to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Faulkner). I would like some indication from the government whether or not they will proceed with the construction of this highway; I do not care where the answer comes from.
1 am not alone in urging the completion of the Liard highway. The Northwest Territories' finance committee is also urging the federal government to complete the Liard highway. In view of the high unemployment rate at the present time, a project such as the Liard highway and the highway which is to be built from Fort McMurray to Fort Smith in the Northwest Territories would provide much needed work. I hope a favourable decision will be reached shortly. I also hope the government will look seriously at the policy recommended by the previous minister of Indian affairs and northern development, and that the policy of northern preference will be adhered to.

department has not been involved.
